**What the Source class determines at the right edge.** In §14.2 Andrews names four classes for the first number slot of the absolutive singular or common form. After the prepared stem, the examples write **a → tl**, **pah → tli**, **cal → li**, **mich → in**, and **chichi → silence**. The **li** of **cal** is part of the **tli** class. Atoms `ACI-P124-L018-CA26E12690`, `ACI-P124-L019-D96493D034`, `ACI-P124-L020-A2364BC0C2`, `ACI-P124-L021-D61F33C5DE`, and `ACI-P124-L022-3C1A86FAB0` record the examples. The writer identifies the stem class. The grammar supplies the ending for the selected state and number. The native menu further distinguishes subclasses. [Canvas §14.2](../../ANDREWS_TRANSCRIPTION_CANVAS.md#L4706) · [Atom ledger](../ANDREWS_ATOM_LEDGER.json) · [Source class menu](../../src/ui/shell/classical_shell.mjs#L786)

**What distinguishes tli 1 and tli 2.** In the possessive singular or common form, the **tli 1** pattern leaves the connector silent and the **tli 2** pattern normally supplies **hui**. Andrews writes **mo → nacaz** and **n → oh → hui** in **monacaz** and **nohhui**. Fresh direct Owner requests reproduced both forms with the corresponding Source classes. The class identifies the connector pattern while the speaker chooses a possessor. The [possessive ending entry](#choosing-whether-a-nominal-predicate-has-a-possessor) describes a limited **tli 2** choice where Andrews also licenses silence. Atoms `ACI-P130-L031-E0C3656D8E` and `ACI-P130-L038-169019F199` record the two examples. [Canvas §14.7.1.b](../../ANDREWS_TRANSCRIPTION_CANVAS.md#L4972) · [Atom ledger](../ANDREWS_ATOM_LEDGER.json)

**Two base-stem subclasses in possession.** With **cihuā** prepared, Andrews’s **nimocihuāuh** writes **ni → mo → cihuā → uh**. The **tl 1-A** class supplies **uh** after the base stem in this possessive form. With **icxi** prepared, **tl 1-B** gives **mo → cxi** in **mocxi**. The supportive initial **i** is absent at the left join and the number connector at the right is silent. The class identifies the pattern before the writer selects State and Possessor. Atoms `ACI-P131-L038-DE66ACF0CF` and `ACI-P132-L015-A9427E12F4` record the two forms. [Canvas 1-A](../../ANDREWS_TRANSCRIPTION_CANVAS.md#L5024) · [Canvas 1-B](../../ANDREWS_TRANSCRIPTION_CANVAS.md#L5044) · [Atom ledger](../ANDREWS_ATOM_LEDGER.json)

**Subclasses that shorten the stem.** The Source menu distinguishes **tl 2-A**, **tl 2-B (final a)**, **tl 2-B (final i)**, and **tl 2-C**. In Andrews’s possessive examples, the writer prepares the longer stem, then Grammar derives **to → mā** from **māi**, **mo → nac** from **naca**, and **no → cax** from **caxi**. In **no → māx-tli**, from **māx-tla**, Grammar drops the last **a** and supplies a supportive **i**. The apparent **tli** at the right edge belongs to the stem in this example. The possessive number connector is silent in all four. The Source choice identifies which pattern to apply. The ledger anchors the forms in Atoms `ACI-P132-L024-3A0441F8E3` (**tomā**), `ACI-P132-L034-0500D8A644` (**monac**), `ACI-P133-L009-B029B88592` (**nocax**), and `ACI-P133-L018-DDC1E4D2B3` (**nomāxtli**). [Atom ledger](../ANDREWS_ATOM_LEDGER.json) A direct ordinary-NNC Owner check with possessive State and a third-common nonhuman subject accepted **tomā**, **monac**, and **nocax** using their documented classes and possessors. The **māx-tla** request stopped at the application authority check, which rejected the `canvasSection` field. Thus **nomāxtli** here is Canvas evidence. The exact public class-selection paths remain unverified. [Canvas §14.7.2.b](../../ANDREWS_TRANSCRIPTION_CANVAS.md#L5052) · [Native class options](../../src/ui/shell/classical_shell.mjs#L800)

The native **Stem formation** label and generated **Stem Formation** appear in ordinary noun Grammar when the exact binding offers stem-relation choices. In the verified **cal** draft it offered **plain**, **affinity**, and **distributive-varietal**. Apply **cal**, choose **Make a noun clause → Animacy → nonanimate**, then choose the formation and Make. On paper, the affinity and distributive choices put **cā-** or **cah-** before the already prepared **cal**. They express houses of one village or houses in separate places or of different kinds. The Owner supplies the spelling and the **-li** after the stem. The binding projects the eligible values into the generated selector. The native **Stem relation** field was hidden in these browser runs. **Predicate Formation** is a second generated selector in ordinary noun Grammar. After opening the choices for applied **cal**, isolated Chrome showed **source-stem** selected, with **yo-matrix** and **analogical-restricted-use** available. The browser observation establishes the captions and default for that draft. Andrews’s **tlamāitl** illustrates why a writer might choose an analogical formation on a suitable stem. Starting from **māi**, the Owner builds **tla → māi → tl**. The supplied nominal stem stays in the middle, and Grammar determines the new prefix and ending from the chosen formation. Atom `ACI-P137-L033-A92CDAFC82` records **tlamā** as the possessive predicate before reranking, and `ACI-P137-L035-8D4624AD77` records **tlamāitl** as the resulting sleeve expression. The position of **tla** stays on the left while its role changes from possessor to part of the new stem. A direct Owner check on **māi** verified the licensed choice and produced **tlamāitl** in absolutive State and **ītlamā** with a third-person possessor. The latter shows the new possessor before the already formed sleeve stem. In isolated Chrome, applying **māi** as an NNC showed the **tl 2 a** class and a possessive draft with a third-singular possessor. The tested sequence was **Grammar → Make a noun clause → Animacy → nonanimate → Predicate Formation → analogical-restricted-use → Make**. It accepted **Ītlamā.** with Linear **#0-0+ī-0(tla-mā)0-0#**, matching the Owner check. A second browser run showed why **State** was initially absent. The default **source-stem** has only possessive State in the exact Owner selection frame. Choosing **analogical-restricted-use** exposed a selector offering **absolutive**. Selecting that value and clicking Make accepted **Tlamāitl.**, with Linear **#0-0(tla-māi)tl-0#**. The direct Owner check confirmed both States become available after the formation choice. This is a writing decision unlocked by the previous choice: after forming the sleeve stem, the writer can use it with a possessor on the left or in the absolutive form with **-tl** on the right. [Source-stem possession policy](../../src/application/classical/nnc_application.mjs#L794) On paper the newly added **ī-** precedes **tla-mā**. The legacy lesson suite’s standalone Node invocation only loads its exported runner; invoking that runner with the headless runtime stopped at the missing formula-annotation helper. **Where to find Predicate Formation.** The ordinary-noun **Predicate Formation** selector builds the stem the writer will use. Choosing **analogical-restricted-use** with **māi** prepared gives the sleeve form **tla → māi → tl** in the absolutive build. Andrews records the formative steps in Atoms `ACI-P137-L033-A92CDAFC82` and `ACI-P137-L035-8D4624AD77`. The native ordinary-noun predicate-form field is assigned to the **Nounstem** group. The organizer also defines a separate nominal disclosure caption **Predicate formation** for a section keyed to Predicate. The default field map assigns no controls to that section. The browser evidence above establishes the generated selector on the ordinary-noun route. The custom placement map routes three deverbal fields to the native Predicate section: **Supplementary object activation**, **Surviving tē in double-object patientive**, and **Patientive referent**. The renderer moves each field into the route-specific lane. On a nominal route it shows the Predicate section when at least one field wrapper in that section is visible. The disclosure mirrors the section’s hidden state. Opening it lets the writer reach whichever choices the current Source licenses. [Section visibility](../../src/ui/rendering/nominal_construction_presentation.mjs#L1044) · [Disclosure visibility](../../src/ui/composition/composition_presentation.mjs#L116) For the favor example, **Patientive referent** lets the writer choose the beneficiary or the favor. ### Possessive number ending for a general-use stem

For a general-use Source whose selection contract supplies singular connector values, Grammar inserts **Choose ending** as the initial prompt in **Possessive number ending** and enables only the options the contract permits. Andrews’s **ītozqui** ‘it is his voice’ has the possessor **ī** at the left, followed by **tozqui**, with no letters at the right-hand number position. After entering **toz-qui** and identifying the possessor, the writer selects **silent** to confirm that the line ends at **qui**. In this exact case, the Owner offers only **silent**. The explicit selection completes the draft. Andrews determines the ending. Example Atom `ACI-P160-L007-CAAE13F7F6` records the full sentence. Schema Atom `ACI-P160-L010-D684A8F450` records the inner formula, including the possessor and the silent slots after **toz-qui**. Its Owner attribution concerns the full sentence’s discontinuous supplementation. The focused ordinary-noun test checks the inner form and its connector separately. [Canonical Atom ledger](../ANDREWS_ATOM_LEDGER.json) All six focused tests passed, including the missing-connector rejection and the exact issued **ītozqui**. The dynamic prompt is verified in renderer code. Its exact public click sequence remains unverified. **Lexicalized whole NNC.** Enter **michin īīx** as a single Source expression. Andrews §35.14 gives it a fixed inner order, **michin → īīx**, and a conventional meaning, ‘wart’. The writer can reuse that whole as the first part of an ownerhood compound. The fixture shows the interface-side admission, stages the Source for Make, and checks that the resulting whole keeps both original nuclei. A later ownerhood operation writes the matrix after them. The Source choice thus preserves already composed material for the next written step. This is renderer and runtime evidence. The public click sequence remains unverified. | State | Ordinary nominal Grammar, for a single-form draft when the Owner offers multiple states | With the nounstem prepared, choose **absolutive** for an expression without a possessor or **possessive** to give the predicate a possessor. The ending **-uh** belongs to the subject number position. The Owner uses the possessive grammar to determine its availability. The writer specifies second-person singular for the included person. The renderer supplies **Choose included person** when none is selected and restricts the options to the Source contract. ## Writing a numeral or a counted unit

| Control | Where and when | Action and inferred purpose | Sweep disposition |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Number | Conditional cardinal Grammar | Supply the quantity. Andrews's **cē** and **cemilhuitl** both express one. | Retain in this pass |
| Count | Conditional cardinal Grammar | Select **ordinary count** or **gross or total count**. With **ōme** prepared, **ōme-n** gives the simple count, while **ōme-x** marks the total. The writer makes the count decision before adding the number ending. | Retain in this pass |
| Plural ending | Conditional ordinary-count Grammar | Choose **t-in** or a silent ending where licensed. Andrews gives **tōmentin ~ tōmen** for ‘we are two in number’. The difference occurs at the right edge. | Retain in this pass |
| Gross-count possessor | Conditional possessive gross-count Grammar | Identify an animate plural possessor or a nonanimate possessor with a plural referent. In Andrews's **imōmextin**, the possessor precedes the numeral and the number ending follows it. | Retain in this pass |
| Nonanimate number spelling | Conditional nonanimate possessive gross-count Grammar | Choose whether to represent final **n**. Andrews records **ti** alongside **tin**, while noting that final **n** was often unwritten. This motivates a spelling choice without establishing that the two spellings always express different grammar. | Retain in this pass |
| Numeral modifier | Conditional cardinal Grammar | Specify approximation or an additional quantity. In **Canah mahtlāctli.**, **canah** comes before ‘ten’ and makes the quantity approximate. In **Oc cē.**, the opening **oc** means ‘another’ or ‘more’. | Retain in this pass |
| Conjunction form | Basic cardinal nominal Grammar for values 11–14, according to the renderer | Choose **separate numeral clauses** or **conjunctive compound**. Andrews describes both ways to add units to ten. | Retain in this pass |
| Numeral use | Conditional cardinal Grammar | Choose **numeral NNC** or **numeral embedded in a VNC**. Andrews gives standalone **cē** and numeral-derived material inside **ticenyāzqueh**. | Retain in this pass |
| Licensed numeral shape | Conditional cardinal Grammar where a shape choice is exposed | Select a licensed form for the intended use. Andrews explains why the stem can lose final **m** outside the embed position and acquire vowel length. That conditioned shape change alone does not imply both forms are selectable in the same context. | Retain in this pass |
| Counting set / Classifier | Native cardinal Grammar and the typed numeral binding, respectively | Identify the kind of unit. For four rows, choose **row**. Andrews writes **nāp → pān → tli**, with row material after the numeral. The grammar supplies the join, including the spelling of **nāp** before **pān**. | Retain in this pass |
| Stem relation | Cardinal Grammar and nominal compound Grammar | Choose an ordinary, affinity, or distributive/varietal stem where licensed. In the numeral example **cēcentetl**, write **cē-** before **cen** for ‘one after another’. In **cehcentetl**, write **ceh-** there for ‘one apiece’. The counting stem **tetl** still follows the numeral. | Retain in this pass |

**Writing the copy in a numeral.** The writer starts with the quantity and counting set, then chooses the intended relation. Canvas §34.14 shows why the two copies differ and describes where the copy falls, including exceptions for certain number stems. Atom `ACI-P332-L003-743D90E1FC` indexes the numeral-reduplication rule. The lesson fixture exercises affinity and distributive requests for several numbers. The exact public options for the matched pair remain unverified. The topology map reports an Owner comparison between the construction with exact **Cē.** and **Ilhuitl.** as inputs and an ordinary typed **cem-ilhui** Source. Both write **Cemilhuitl.** The exact numeral-day construction preserves the two pieces for the later temporal derivation. With several compatible sets, the writer can choose among them. For a prepared numeral and a referent known to require the row set, the next written piece in **nāppāntli** is therefore determined by that analysis. If the referent leaves the grouping open, **Counting set** supplies the writer’s intended unit. The renderer rule and Owner compatibility gate establish this distinction. **Choosing the numeral's use and spelling.** With **Number** set to one, **Numeral use** offers **numeral NNC** or **numeral embedded in a VNC**. For a genuine spelling choice, start with free three. **Licensed numeral shape** offers **free form · ēyi** or **free form with initial y · yēyi**. The writer chooses whether to put **y** before **ēyi**. Atom `ACI-P324-L018-14A1E117F1` records both forms. The native renderer switches its list between free and embedded numeral contexts. An embedded **two** offers **short embed · ōm with assimilation** and **full embed · ōme**. Andrews writes the short material at the start of **ōmilhuitl**. In **nitlaōmetēma** the writer has **ni → tla** on the page when reaching the full **ōme** before **tēma**. Embedded **three** offers **embed with y lost · ē**, **embed with y retained · yē**, and **embed with y realized as x · ēx**. Andrews illustrates the embedded result in **ēilhuitl** and **ēxihuitl**. The displayed options identify the shape of the upcoming numeral inside the word. The different host examples show how the shapes occur, and the controls depend on the exact choice inventory for the draft. In a higher-order numeral the renderer checks the first term’s multiplier, so forty can expose embedded **two** and sixty embedded **three**. ### Measuring an amount or distance

| Control | Where and when | Action and inferred purpose | Sweep disposition |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Measure meaning | Conditional cardinal measure Grammar | Choose amount or length. Andrews contrasts expressions such as **cencamatl** ‘one mouthful’ and **cemmecatl** ‘one rope length’. | Retain in this pass |
| Measure nounstem class | Same measure group | Identify the class of the unit that follows the numeral in the compound, such as the **tl** class of **cama** in **cencamatl**. | Retain in this pass |
| Measure result | Same measure group | Choose the measure alone or include the thing measured on its right. For a marked join with **in**, see the separate [Modifier adjunctor](#placing-an-adjective-or-a-describing-clause) route, checked with the same load and food. | Retain in this pass |
| Measured nounstem class | Nominal Grammar after **Counting set → measure** and **Measure result → measure with thing measured** | With **centlamāmalli** ‘one load’ prepared, supply the food stem **tlacuāl** and select its **tli** class. The Owner writes that noun after the load, with its own **li** ending. This class describes the food, while **Measure nounstem class** describes the load. [Canvas §34.16](../../ANDREWS_TRANSCRIPTION_CANVAS.md#L12724) · [Measured constituent Atom `ACI-P333-L034-24B2AA08CD-05`](../ANDREWS_ATOM_LEDGER.json) · [Separate request field](../../src/ui/rendering/nominal_construction_presentation.mjs#L9431) · [Owner realization](../../src/core/classical/nominal_construction.mjs#L13554) | Retain in this pass |

**Writing order.** With one selected, the writer supplies the measure unit and its class. **Measure meaning → amount or quantity** describes what is counted in **cen → cama → tl** ‘one mouthful’. **Length or distance** describes the use of the unit in **cem → meca → tl** ‘one rope length’. Atoms `ACI-P333-L012-756B192497` and `ACI-P333-L028-6E553EDCE1` record these uses. The unit and class choices give the grammar the material and ending after the numeral. Once the measure **centlamāmalli** is ready, **Measure result → measure with thing measured** reveals **Measured nounstem class**. This supplies the class for the second noun, **tlacuāl**, whose written form follows the measure. In **Quimacah centlamāmalli in tlacualli.**, Andrews writes **in** at that boundary. Atom `ACI-P333-L034-24B2AA08CD-05` identifies the measure as principal and the food as the thing measured. The focused Owner fixture passed for measures and for the composed measure-plus-food structure. A direct comparison from the same unit inputs produced **Centlamāmalli.** with **measure NNC only** and **centlamāmalli tlacuālli.** with **measure with thing measured**. Omitting the measured class in the combined request blocked it. The combined Owner frame identifies the second NNC as **thing-measured-nnc**. That projection joins the two surfaces with a space. The cited Canvas sentence writes overt **in** at that join and has a different written vowel quantity in **tlacualli**. The measurements verify the scope of the existing choice. The exact Canvas wording requires evidence beyond this combined projection. [Owner combination and spelling](../../src/core/classical/nominal_construction.mjs#L13552) The full sentence remains unverified in the browser.

**The two stem fields and their written positions.** The combined-measure request uses **Matrix** as the unit stem and **Embed** as the measured stem. Thus the writer can enter **tlacuāl** in **Embed** even though the food is written after the load, whose unit stem is entered in **Matrix**. **Counting set → measure** opens the measure settings. **Measure result → measure with thing measured** opens **Measured nounstem class**, and the Owner requires both the measured stem and its class for the combined draft. Contextual captions such as **Unit of measure** and **Thing measured** could show which role each existing field serves. A staged readout could put the measure first and the measured noun second. These are design inferences from the native request and Andrews’s written order. The exact public interaction remains unverified. **The boundary after the measure.** Andrews §42.8 also gives unmarked **centlaxōchtli ichcatl** and **nāuhtlayahualōlli centli**. The separate adjectival-modification Owner projects **Modifier adjunctor** from its topology and licensed axes. This verifies that the existing decision can place **in** immediately after the measure and before the food. The check covers the two-noun construction. The examples illustrate different attested dates. They do not establish both choices for every numeral–day-sign pair.

### Naming from a calendar expression

**Naming from a day sign or using a calendar expression to name a thing.** The personal-name **Source structure** field also defines **calendar · day sign** and **calendar · personalizing a thing**. The first uses an eligible day sign as the prepared naming material, as in **Cipac → tōnal**. The second uses the calendar expression as a name for a thing, as in **Xōchi → tōnal**. Andrews gives **Xōchitōnal** as the name of the creature guarding the approach to Mictlan. Atoms `ACI-P620-L025-B125DD1391-02` and `ACI-P620-L027-767A78FD22` establish the first name’s internal form and the second’s personalizing use. At this step the constituent order is already supplied by the prepared expression. The choice tells the name Owner how to reuse it. The tests for the two exact compound inputs passed and verified the written names. The labels and Owner eligibility are verified in code. Exact browser selection remains unverified. [Canvas §56.3.5](../../ANDREWS_TRANSCRIPTION_CANVAS.md#L24605) · [Option labels](../../src/ui/shell/classical_shell.mjs#L1252) · [Exact Source eligibility](../../src/core/nnc/names/names.mjs#L890) · [Caiman fixture](../../src/tests/reader_56_3_caiman_explicit_day_name.test.mjs) · [Flower fixture](../../src/tests/reader_56_3_flower_day_thing_name.test.mjs) · [Atom ledger](../ANDREWS_ATOM_LEDGER.json)

**Reusing Five Flower as the first piece of a place name.** The passing fixture keeps the exact **Mācuilxōchitl** personal-name Result as the input to the adverbial place-name formation. The writer carries forward **Mācuilxōchi** and adds **-c** at the right edge, yielding Andrews’s **Mācuilxōchic**. The Owner silences the inner absolutive ending in that construction and rejects **-co** for this exact name. The date by itself is also rejected by the tested place-name request. This traces three writing decisions in order: assemble the date, use it as a personal name, then use that name in a place name. The exact runtime fixture verifies the handoffs. The equivalent public sequence through **Date spelling**, personal-name Grammar, and **Formation** remains unverified. **Deciding where to write the adjunctor.** Canvas §56.5 gives three uses of the same conjoined name. After writing the lead-in, the writer can put **in → Tloqueh → in → Nāhuaqueh** on the page, write **in → Tloqueh → Nāhuaqueh**, or write **Tloqueh → Nāhuaqueh**. Each choice changes whether there is an **in** before the first name or between the names. **Applying an honorific to a completed name.** With **ītz-cuāuh** prepared, **Affective operation → apply to the complete outer name** makes the complete name the target of the honorific. **Affective matrix → tzin** supplies the material that follows it. Andrews’s Golden Eagle formula shows the grammar silencing the earlier inner **tli** and writing **ītz-cuāuh → tzin**. Atom `ACI-P617-L022-A7A8014595-04` records **tzin** as the honorific matrix. The focused Owner test passed both the honorific **Ītzcuāuhtzin** and the plain **Ītzcuāuhtli** with the same exact compound parent. Andrews’s **tīxtlilton** illustrates another matrix, **ton**, for a different name (Atom `ACI-P617-L025-80B8BCA3BE`). The renderer first filters **Affective operation** by the chosen Source structure. A quoted citation offers **none**. The structured families normally include **apply to the complete outer name**. Eligible nominal families can also offer **apply within the inner source**, and the two preterit-agentive families can offer **general-use agentive honorific**. The renderer clears an incompatible scope to **none**. It shows **Affective matrix** when the scope is active and filters **tzin**, **tz**, and **ton** against the Owner axis. With **Ītzcuāuhtli** prepared, the outer operation applies respect to the complete name, so the writer reaches the right edge of the named material before writing **tzin**. The other scope labels serve their own Source families. [Source-family scope inventory](../../src/core/nnc/names/names.mjs#L294) · [Native labels](../../src/ui/shell/classical_shell.mjs#L1280) The examples establish the written position of the matrix for their own names. Exact public choices for the alternative scopes remain open. ## Writing a place name or a name for its inhabitants

| Control | Where and when | Action and inferred purpose | Sweep disposition |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Place / gentilic result | Place and gentilic Grammar when a compatible Source or exact saved Result opens the operation | With **Mēxihco** prepared, select **gentilic** if the next expression names a person associated with the place. That choice opens the applicable formation. The later choices write **ni → Mēxih → ca → tl**. Andrews distinguishes the place name from the person named by its derivative. [Canvas §48.9](../../ANDREWS_TRANSCRIPTION_CANVAS.md#L20500) · [Public and Owner evidence below](#writing-a-place-name-or-a-name-for-its-inhabitants) | Retain in this pass |
| Formation | Place or gentilic Grammar after selecting an output kind, when the current input supplies eligible formations | With **Mēxihco** prepared, select the gentilic output, then the licensed **co/c replacement + ca** formation. The writer keeps **Mēxih** and the grammar replaces the old location ending with **ca** before the final **tl** in **ni → Mēxih → ca → tl**. The same selector offers different patterns for other bases. [Canvas §48.9.4](../../ANDREWS_TRANSCRIPTION_CANVAS.md#L20442) · [Output and input filtering](../../src/ui/rendering/nominal_construction_presentation.mjs#L5760) | Retain in this pass |
| Place matrix | Gentilic Grammar after choosing **co/c replacement + ca** | Identify the old ending in the prepared place name. Choose **co** for **Mēxihco** and **c** for **Tecōāc**. This choice describes what is already at the right edge; the formation silences it and supplies **ca**. The two written examples read **ni → Mēxih → ca → tl** and **ni → Tecōā → ca → tl**. [Canvas §48.9.4.b.i](../../ANDREWS_TRANSCRIPTION_CANVAS.md#L20500) · [Exact Source check](../../src/core/nnc/place_gentilic/place_gentilic.mjs#L2496) | Retain in this pass |
| Structural analysis | Place-name Grammar after choosing **place + tzin/tōn + co** | With **Ātōya** prepared, choose whether it represents a place name or an affective nounstem. Both readings of **Ātōyatzinco** write **Ātōya → tzin → co**. The place-name reading has an old locative ending that stays silent. The writer selects the intended Source, and the Owner supplies the corresponding boundary. [Canvas](../../ANDREWS_TRANSCRIPTION_CANVAS.md#L20277) · [Field visibility](../../src/ui/rendering/nominal_construction_presentation.mjs#L5830) | Retain in this pass |
| Affective matrix (place) | Place-name Grammar for **place + tzin/tōn + co** or the gentilic-based affective place formation | Choose the affective material before the final **co**. In **Ātōyatzinco**, **tzin** follows **Ātōya**. Andrews’s **Iztapantōnco** witnesses **tōn** for another prepared base. Each is a Canvas example of its own form. [Canvas affective place names](../../ANDREWS_TRANSCRIPTION_CANVAS.md#L20277) · [Field visibility](../../src/ui/rendering/nominal_construction_presentation.mjs#L5834) | Retain in this pass |
| Profession / title record | Place and gentilic Grammar for **profession-place-association** or **profession-pertinency** | After choosing the profession route, select **Toltec craftsman** to supply **tōltēca**. With first-person plural and absolutive State, write **ti → tōltēca → h**. With the possessive example, the same record occupies the middle of **am → i → tōltēca → huān**. The writer selects the record separately from the person and State that affect both edges. [Canvas §48.13](../../ANDREWS_TRANSCRIPTION_CANVAS.md#L20667) · [Owner record captions](../../src/core/nnc/place_gentilic/ui_contract.mjs#L130) · [Visibility](../../src/ui/rendering/nominal_construction_presentation.mjs#L5839) | Retain in this pass |

**What Formation changes on the page.** Andrews gives four principal patterns. The menu uses labels for those patterns and for individual subtypes.

| Menu example | What the writer has and what follows |
| --- | --- |
| **nonlocative tribal gentilic** | With **Otomi** prepared, write **n → Otomi → tl** in **nOtomitl**. The ordinary nominal ending follows the tribal stem. [Canvas §48.9.1](../../ANDREWS_TRANSCRIPTION_CANVAS.md#L20369) |
| **two-clause gentilic** | After **Ātlacuīhuayān**, write **nitlācatl** to name the dweller. The place comes before the second clause. Andrews also describes writing the two clauses solid. [Canvas §48.9.2](../../ANDREWS_TRANSCRIPTION_CANVAS.md#L20376) |
| **ownerhood agentive gentilic** | From **Āmaquemehcān**, use the ownerhood agentive inside the place name. In **nĀmaquemeh**, write the subject before the recovered agentive and leave the locative material out. [Canvas §48.9.3](../../ANDREWS_TRANSCRIPTION_CANVAS.md#L20412) |
| **other agentive gentilic** | From **Tolohcan**, use the preterit agentive of ‘bow one’s head’. Write **ni → Tōloh** for the singular and **ti → Tōloh → queh** for the plural. The locative part of the original place name is outside this gentilic. [Canvas §48.9.3.b](../../ANDREWS_TRANSCRIPTION_CANVAS.md#L20427) · [Owner formation branch](../../src/core/nnc/place_gentilic/place_gentilic.mjs#L2470) |
| **co/c replacement + ca** | With **Mēxihco** prepared, write **ni → Mēxih → ca → tl**. The old place ending stays unwritten and **ca** marks association with the place. [Canvas §48.9.4](../../ANDREWS_TRANSCRIPTION_CANVAS.md#L20442) · [Replacement example](../../ANDREWS_TRANSCRIPTION_CANVAS.md#L20500) |

For the **-ca** family, the Source determines which boundary the writer needs to describe.

| Formation option | Andrews example and written change |
| --- | --- |
| **full place + ca** | **Huexōtlah** supplies the whole place stem before **ca → tl**. [Canvas §48.9.4.a.i](../../ANDREWS_TRANSCRIPTION_CANVAS.md#L20451) |
| **pan + ē-ca** | In **nIztapanēcatl**, **pan** remains written, then **ē → ca → tl** follows it. [Canvas §48.9.4.a.ii](../../ANDREWS_TRANSCRIPTION_CANVAS.md#L20458) |
| **cā-n + m-ē-ca** | In the **Xaltocan** example, the old final **n** becomes **m** before **ē-ca**. [Canvas §48.9.4.a.ii](../../ANDREWS_TRANSCRIPTION_CANVAS.md#L20482) |
| **ownerhood cā-n replacement + ca** | In **nĀmaquemehcatl**, the Owner retains **Āmaquemeh** and supplies **ca → tl** where the old locative ending was. [Canvas §48.9.4.b.ii](../../ANDREWS_TRANSCRIPTION_CANVAS.md#L20525) |
| **mā-n/tlā-n → mē-ca/tē-ca** | In the **Olman** example, the written place ending gives way to **me-ca** before the nominal ending. [Canvas §48.9.4.b.iii](../../ANDREWS_TRANSCRIPTION_CANVAS.md#L20540) |

The rows match the contractual captions to Andrews’s written examples. A focused run of nine §48.9 fixture files passed all 75 cases. The cases cover tribal stems, two-clause concatenation, both agentive families, and the five **-ca** formation branches. They check written outputs under exact Owner requests. They do not establish that every corresponding option is shown on the public menu for each Source. [Focused runtime receipt](/tmp/ui-intent-gentilic-fixtures.log) The exact public options still depend on the Source offered to the binding. [Formation option contract](../../src/core/nnc/place_gentilic/ui_contract.mjs#L102)

**Choosing the output before its ending.** With an exact saved Result, **Place / gentilic result** prompts **Choose a place or gentilic Result**. Changing the output kind filters **Formation**. For an exact saved Result, the renderer clears the old formation when it detects a different output kind. The formation prompt reads **Choose the Result kind first** or **Choose a formation**. In Andrews’s **Mēxihco → niMēxihcatl**, the writer uses the earlier place as Source, writes **ni-** before the place-derived stem, and writes **-ca-tl** at the right after the original **-co** goes silent. The two controls let the writer identify the intended output and then its licensed formation. The prompt and reset behavior are established by the renderer. The exact browser switch remains unverified. [Canvas §48.9](../../ANDREWS_TRANSCRIPTION_CANVAS.md#L20500) · [Output and formation prompts](../../src/ui/rendering/nominal_construction_presentation.mjs#L5750)

**Place choices from an exact typed Source.** When the typed binding recognizes a place nominal Source, it shows the ordinary **Place / gentilic result** and **Formation** fields. It hides and disables entries outside the Owner’s projection. This route offers **place-name** and **n-cān**, with both selections required. With no staged values, the menus prompt for a Result kind and a formation. Clearing the binding restores the saved visibility and disabled state of the ordinary options. Andrews’s **Cochtocān** shows the writing action. The writer prepares **coch → to** as a site compound, then writes **cān** after it. Atom `ACI-P512-L032-843B1C0F3E-03` assigns the site-compound derivation to the place formation Owner, and `ACI-P512-L032-843B1C0F3E-08` identifies **coch** as the patientive noun ‘sleep’. A fresh run of the eight §48.2.5 cases passed, including **Cochtocān**. [Atom ledger](../ANDREWS_ATOM_LEDGER.json) · [Focused place-name tests](../../src/tests/reader_48_2_5_nominal_place_names.test.mjs) The Owner limits formation to this path for the recognized Source. In the typed projection, both menus start at their prompts and each has one authorized value. A readout beside **Formation** could say **coch → to → cān**, so the writer can see what the required selection will put after the already prepared compound. The current interface still requires the explicit **place-name** and **n-cān** selections before Make. Before both are selected, the binding exposes only allowed values and the missing-choice IDs. Once ready, it evaluates the exact request for authorization and returns that request, with no written preview in the binding. A direct runtime check held **coch → to** fixed. With neither field selected, the binding reported both choices missing. With only **place-name**, it reported **formation** missing. In both states it returned no executable request. With **n-cān** also selected, a separate Owner evaluation of the returned request yielded **cochtocān** without accepting a Result. This verifies the three draft states at the Owner boundary. A written readout could reuse that Owner evaluation after both selections. [Binding readiness and preflight](../../src/core/nnc/place_gentilic/place_gentilic.mjs#L1596) · [Preview and Make fixture](../../src/tests/reader_48_2_5_nominal_place_names.test.mjs#L48) This is a proposal based on Canvas and the one-option projection. The visibility rules are from code, and the exact browser sequence remains open. [Canvas §48](../../ANDREWS_TRANSCRIPTION_CANVAS.md#L20124) · [Exact Source and required choices](../../src/core/nnc/place_gentilic/place_gentilic.mjs#L1563) · [Typed place menus](../../src/ui/rendering/owner_journey_presentation.mjs#L435) · [Menu restoration](../../src/ui/rendering/owner_journey_presentation.mjs#L226)

**Formation choices that require a saved verb.** The renderer filters formations by output kind and, for an exact verbal Result, by the Owner’s available formations for that Result. Hidden options are also disabled. The **n · active imperfect predicate** and **n · nonactive imperfect predicate** entries are excluded without an exact verbal Result. Andrews’s **Ātl-Īhuetziyān** uses active imperfect material before the final place-forming **n**. **Tepanōhuayān** carries nonactive **hua** before **yā → n**. The choice takes a prepared predicate as its left-hand material. Its voice and tense determine whether the exact option is offered. The code establishes the filter. Seven focused §48.2.1 tests passed for the active and nonactive families. The water-fall fixture first builds the possessed locative and combines it with the water noun, then submits that exact nominal composition to the Owner. It produces **Ātlīhuetziyān**, where Canvas has **Ātl-Īhuetziyān**. **Tepanōhuayān** uses its exact saved impersonal imperfect verb. The panel’s verbal-only filter therefore describes its entry path, while the active Owner also accepts an exact nominal composition. An in-memory probe added the same capability-navigation inspection the workbench uses to the water and Huaxtec fixtures. For both exact nominal compositions, it returned **missing prerequisite** and no validated place-name binding, even though the direct Owner formation still passed. This places the observed gap before the writer can choose the final **n** formation. In contrast, a matching probe on the three saved nonactive imperfect verbs returned an available, validated place-name binding and exactly **n-imperfect-nonactive** as the compatible formation. For **Tepanōhuayān**, this connects the prepared **tepanōhuaya** predicate to the final place-forming **n** through the existing control. Atom `ACI-P510-L011-67833D48FE` records the rule that the locative **n** takes nominalized imperfect material. Atom `ACI-P510-L028-B689343E7E` records the **Tepanōhuayān** example. The prepared verb contributes the nonactive **hua**. In the written place name the grammar realizes **hua → yā → n** at the right edge. A cue on **Formation** could show the pending **-yān** ending from the prepared verb without asking the writer to choose its voice again. [Canonical Atom ledger](../ANDREWS_ATOM_LEDGER.json) These probes check navigator and Owner data. The browser interactions remain open. **What happened when reopening the nonactive predicate.** An isolated Chrome run opened an Owner-generated address for the prepared impersonal imperfect **tepanōhuaya**, selected **Analysis**, and visited **Result**. The public replay displayed **Tepanōya**, without the expected **hua**. After **Continue entire Result** timed out, the same tab settled with **Tepanōya** still accepted, no available place-name entry in the Build menu, and Make disabled. This run reached neither the **Formation** selector nor the place name. It identifies a visible difference at replay before the control under study. An independent fresh-runtime round trip reproduced the same switch: the original exact Result was impersonal **tepanōhuaya**, and import yielded active **tepanōya**. The serialized finite application kept the stem, class, valence, subject, mood, and tense but carried neither the requested voice nor the selected **hua** option. This locates the loss for the tested address before the browser can present **Formation**. It leaves open what the interface offers when the exact nonactive verb is made in the same session. **Why the saved verb fixes the voice here.** For the verbal continuation, the place-name resolver checks the exact issued clause, an imperfect request, and the imperfect tense slot. Active and inherently impersonal sources map to the active formation. Passive and impersonal sources map to the nonactive formation. In **Tepanōhuayān**, the saved impersonal **tepanōhuaya** already supplies **hua**. The writer chooses to form a place name, and the resolver derives which imperfect formation is available from that Source. Choosing **Formation** cannot change the voice inside the predicate. The focused nonactive fixture also checks that entering a stem alone or requesting active formation from this saved verb is blocked. **When Place matrix is needed.** The renderer shows **Place matrix** only for **gentilic** with the formation caption **co/c replacement + ca**. The choice identifies which old locative ending the writer starts from. In **Mēxihco → niMēxihcatl**, the relevant old ending is **co** and is silent in the new form. In the source, **co** followed **Mēxih**. In the gentilic, **ca** follows the place-derived material. The existing selectors separate the old ending from the formation that gives the new ending. Andrews’s **Tecōāc → niTecōācatl** uses the same formation with **Place matrix → c**. Atoms `ACI-P521-L025-E7BF9BE35B` and `ACI-P521-L034-64ECB28286` record the **co** and **c** contrasts. All 15 focused tests passed, including singular and plural forms from both exact parents. The Owner checks the selected **co** or **c** against the actual Source ending before writing **ca**. This is a Source classification that makes the later change possible. **Writing one inhabitant or several.** The inflected gentilic route exposes **Person** and **Number**. With **Tecōāc** prepared and **c** identified as its old ending, the same Owner formation gives **ni → Tecōā → ca → tl** for one speaker and **ti → Tecōā → ca → h** for several. The focused fixture holds the exact place fixed and checks the new material at both edges. **Choosing what the affective ending belongs to.** With **place-name** and **place + tzin/tōn + co** active, the renderer offers **Structural analysis** and **Affective matrix**. For **Ātōyatzinco**, **Structural analysis** distinguishes building on an affective noun meaning ‘little river’ from applying the affective formation to a place name. **Affective matrix** supplies **tzin** before the final **co**. Both paths write **Ātōya → tzin → co**, while the place-base formula includes a silent old ending before **tzin**. Andrews says historical information can distinguish the readings. The field begins at **analysis required** and offers **place name + affective** and **affective nounstem + co**. The owner blocks a request with neither analysis selected. A short explanation beside the existing choices could show **old co becomes silent → tzin → co** for the place-name reading and **already affective nounstem → co** for the little-river reading. Atom `ACI-P516-L022-721A8324F1` assigns the historical distinction to the affective ambiguity Owner. The writer can use historical information, when available, to decide which Source they intend. The grammar supplies the silence when that Source is the place name. **Other outputs in Place / gentilic result.** The option contract also names **gentilic collectivity**, **profession or title**, **profession pertinency**, and **adjectival gentilic use**. For **Mēxihcayōtl**, Andrews puts **yō** after the gentilic stem to express the people collectively or what is characteristic of them. For **āmantēcayōtl**, the already prepared profession stem comes before **yō**, which yields a word for feather working. **Shared controls on the place and gentilic routes.** The native renderer makes **Person**, **Number**, **Animacy**, **Humanness**, and **Output scope** locally available for gentilic, gentilic collectivity, profession or title, and adjectival gentilic use. It separately exposes **State** for collectivity and profession or title, and **Possessor** for those two when State is possessive. **Written order.** The place name writes the identifying material before **-co**. In **niMēxihcatl**, the subject marker precedes the place-derived material and the gentilic matrix follows it. **How the new expression will be used.** In the inspected nominal Grammar request, **Place / gentilic result** sets the construction kind and supplies adverbial usage for a place-name request or ordinary usage for a gentilic. **Formation** and **Place matrix** have separate values. In the **Mēxihco → niMēxihcatl** contrast, the writer identifies the old **-co** and requests the gentilic pattern. Andrews also uses **Mēxihco** as an ordinary nominal expression in **Aoc īc yez in Mēxihco**, which a separate runtime fixture builds. That ordinary use is evidence from Canvas and the Owner. The request mapping describes the inspected UI path’s default usage, and public selection of the ordinary use still needs verification. In the second, it directly supplies the path of the motion. Atoms `ACI-P509-L006-110B56A9C6` and `ACI-P509-L015-BEACB0371D` record both. The name is the writer’s first piece in either case. The intended use tells the writer whether **īc** comes next. All 13 focused place-role tests passed, including both exact lines. The inspected place-name menu requests adverbial usage. ## Setting a nominal clause's position

| Control | Where and when | Action and inferred purpose | Sweep disposition |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Clause position | Conditional nominal Grammar control | Choose **initial** or **noninitial** to describe where the unit will sit in the sentence. This supplies context even while the writer prepares the unit by itself. | Retain in this pass |

**Canvas and written order.** In **Cān in titēquiti?**, interrogative **cān** stands at the left edge. Andrews contrasts this with **zā zo cān**, where **cān** occurs later and means ‘anywhere’ in the expression. Position participates in the reading. This is a Canvas contrast illustrating the purpose of the setting, rather than a claim that the same picker builds both forms.

**A position choice sets up the later join.** The focused Owner fixture first prepared **cān** with **Clause position → noninitial**, then supplied the exact particle **zā zo**. The Owner accepted **Zā zo cān** with indefinite-place scope and retained both inputs. From left to right the writer puts down **zā → zo → cān**. The fixture prepares the last piece first. Position tells the grammar how to treat **cān** when it is joined to the particle. Atoms `ACI-P472-L028-0A1A4EAAE2` and `ACI-P472-L035-57AE8905AC` record the initial question and noninitial indefinite example. The focused test passed. **Public and Owner evidence.** The topology map reports **noninitial** selected in the public **Īmpan.** journey along with a third-plural possessor. That example demonstrates entering position as context on a relational route. The nominal Owner adapter separately carries the sentence-position choice for the relational Source. In isolated Chrome, **Analysis → NNC nominal → Stem: cān → relational n → Embedded source formation: interrogative cā-n** left **Clause position** hidden in Source. After **Use this Source → Grammar → Build a relational noun**, the field became visible with **initial** and **noninitial**, and **noninitial** could be staged. The browser check covers that choice in the draft. The Owner fixture covers assembling **Zā zo cān**.

**Subject reference can change who the line refers to while keeping its agreement shape.** In Andrews’s gathering sentence, write **Ōcenquīz → in ixquich → in tēlpōchtli → in ichpōchtli**. Atom `ACI-P560-L037-6C920D15D3-04` identifies **ixquich** as the supplementary human subject that refers back to the subject of **ōcenquīz**. The writer can represent that generic group when preparing the verb and noun pieces. The exact bindings tested for **tēlpōchtli**, **ixquich**, and **cen-quīza** expose the generic choice and retain common number with third-singular morphological agreement. This choice does not require adding a visible plural suffix. Two focused binding tests passed. The renderer supplies the caption **Subject reference**. In isolated Chrome, type **tēlpōch**, choose **Nounstem class → tli 1**, apply Source, and choose **Grammar → Make a noun clause → Subject reference**. The options were **Ordinary Subject choices** and **Human generic · common number**. Choosing the latter and clicking Make accepted **Tēlpōchtli.** with Linear **#0-0(tēlpōch)tli-0#**. In a separate isolated run from the same **tēlpōch** and class, **Ordinary Subject choices** exposed **Person**, **Number**, **Animacy**, and **Humanness**. Making the unchanged ordinary draft also produced **Tēlpōchtli.** and the same Linear formula. Thus the writer can pick a different kind of reference while keeping the written shape. The browser verifies the menus and the shared form. The binding tests establish the distinct participant metadata. In another isolated Chrome run, **cen-quīza**, Class B, followed by **Make a verb clause → Subject reference → Human generic · common number**, accepted **Cenquīza** in the default present draft. The same two reference options were visible as on the noun. A follow-up opened the **Mood and tense** disclosure, chose **Tense → preterit** with the same generic reference, and made **Cenquīz**. The tense choice changes the right edge of **cen-quīza**. Andrews’s full example has an additional **ō** at the left edge. A third isolated run used the mounted **Continue entire Result** and **Grammar** buttons, selected **Make a sentence**, and toggled **Antecessive ō#**. The box was checked while **Cenquīz** stayed accepted. Explicit Make displayed **Ōcenquīz.** In click order the writer first chose preterit, which affects the right edge, and then added the prefix at the left edge. The following generic group in Andrews’s complete sentence was not staged in this browser run. **Attaching the words that name the group.** **Subject reference** prepares the reference of each piece. A separate Grammar step supplies the group itself. The controller fixture first builds **ixquich → in tēlpōchtli** as a head followed by a shared-subject modifier. It then places that group after **Ōcenquīz**, using **in**, principal-first order, and subject-to-subject supplementation. The staged contract leaves the pieces separate until execution, which makes **Ōcenquīz in ixquich in tēlpōchtli.** and retains common reference with singular agreement at both contact points. That first fixture uses the youth phrase alone. A second focused controller fixture verified the full **Ōcenquīz in ixquich in tēlpōchtli in ichpōchtli.** It attached **in** to each noun, joined the two marked members with unmarked additive conjunction at the adjoined level, used their group as the rightward description of **ixquich**, then attached **ixquich** and its description after the verb as a shared subject. In written order the three occurrences of **in** introduce **ixquich**, **tēlpōchtli**, and **ichpōchtli** in turn. These are controller steps, with public clicks verified only for the individual preparations described above. **Person and Number can change both ends of a noun form.** Andrews’s Appendix B gives first singular **ni → cōl → li** and first plural **ti → cōl → t → in**. The writer keeps the same stem. Changing **Number** from singular to plural in first person changes the material before **cōl** as well as the ending after it. The nominal contract derives the **Person** options from the admitted subjects, then filters **Number** to the selected person’s admitted forms. Either control becomes actionable only when it offers a choice, and the full paradigm enumerates these coordinates. The interface can therefore collect two choices and realize them together on both sides of the stem. This example is Canvas and renderer evidence. The exact browser edit from singular to plural remains unverified. **Choosing the referent before choosing a nominal ending.** Appendix B contrasts the nonanimate **amox → tli** ‘book’, the nonhuman animate **cih → tli** ‘jackrabbit’, and human **ni → cōl → li** ‘I am a grandfather’. For the rabbit plural the writer puts the copy before **cih** and writes **t-in** after it. The book paradigm lacks the corresponding plural-subject series. The human paradigm also permits the first-person prefix before **cōl**. Thus **Animacy** and **Humanness** help determine the subject and number forms the writer can use around the stem. Section 4.6 supplies the general distinctions behind the examples. Atom `ACI-P063-L031-D2FAEC26EB` records that human implies animate and that nonhuman can have either animacy. Atoms `ACI-P063-L032-8A7A37DE90` and `ACI-P063-L032-A84AF59B14` distinguish first and second person from context-dependent third person. The nominal contract derives nonhuman for a nonanimate subject and human for first or second person. If both humanness values are available and the writer has supplied neither, the contract records unspecified. The Appendix B examples give the written forms. The §4.6 Atoms establish the participant distinctions. The separate Atom `ACI-P128-L032-0542CE300B-05` records **cīcihtin** ‘they are jackrabbits’. Focused Owner requests produced nonanimate **amoxtli**, nonhuman animate plural **cīcihtin** with affinity and **t-in**, and first-person human **nicōlli**. Here the writer’s referent and subject choices affect the available material before and after the stem. ## Adding an object through verbal derivation

With a first-person plural reflexive object prepared, Andrews assigns the same **t-o** (or **t-⎕**) before the verbstem both “ourselves” and “one another.” **Object meaning** records which relation the writer intends at that position. Atom `ACI-P075-L003-BBF5D7EC0B` records the shared form, and `ACI-P075-L004-A99BF9D40A-10` records the plural condition on the reciprocal reading. The application fixture contrasts singular **itta** with a reflexive object against plural **itta** with both reflexive and reciprocal readings. The source and template support the distinction. Whether the public workflow exposes a separate choice for that exact plural case is unverified. **Choosing the causer and reading the causee.** With **quīza** prepared as “he leaves,” **Imported subject (causer) → 2sg** puts **ti-** at the left of **ticquīxtia**. The old third-person subject becomes the causee **c**, immediately after **ti**. The **Causee Valence** menu calls this **specific participant · fixed source subject**. For Andrews’s same-person **ninoquīxtia**, **no** follows **ni** and refers to that same person. The focused shared-Owner fixture passed for both coordinate patterns. A retained public imperfect causative using **itt-a** preserved the separate first-person Source subject and third-person causer. Its accepted control frame marked the causee choice ineligible, which illustrates why the menu can be absent when the grammar fixes that representation. This observation concerns the **itt-a** build. The exact **quīza** clicks remain unverified. In the native Grammar renderer, **Imported subject (causer)** requires an authorized causative Source. **Causee Valence** requires that same Source plus the Owner’s causee-choice flag. The latter can therefore disappear while **Imported subject (causer)** remains available. In the verified runtime continuation from **quīxohua**, **ti-** expresses the selected causer and the impersonal Source supplies nonspecific **tē-**. Compare the specific **c** in **ticquīxtia** from the active Source. The source and result may use the same **quīx-tia** stem with different material before it. **Causee realization in a typed draft.** When an exact typed causative binding requires the causee kind, the generated Grammar field is labeled **Causee realization**. The corresponding native continuation field is **Causee Valence**. The Owner asks for this choice when the current derivation needs it. With **quīza** already prepared, the question is how to write the person made to leave after the causer prefix. In **ti → c → quīx → tia**, **c** represents the specific Source subject. In **ni → no → quīx → tia**, **no** represents the person causing themself to leave. The different causer prefixes come from the subject choice. The typed caption and required-choice gate are verified in code. The earlier public causative record verifies a state where the causee choice was ineligible, and the generated field’s exact public use remains open. **An object can remain part of the sentence without letters.** In Andrews's **tinēchchihualtia**, the writer starts from **nicchihua** ‘I make it’ and adds the meaning ‘you cause me to’. On the page, **ti → nēch → chīhualtia**. The original object ‘it’ still belongs to the verb but is silent between **nēch** and the stem in this construction. Starting each request without a preceding eligible draft produced the silent form and left the explicit selection unset in both cases. | Control | Where and when | Action and inferred purpose | Sweep disposition |

| Irregular Result | Verbal Grammar when the authorized Lesson 11 plan supplies more than one stem realization | Choose the preferred form or an attested alternative. ## Choosing verbal voice


**Patient fields for an already nonactive stem.** A typed nonactive carrier can expose **Patient agreement**, **Patient animacy**, **Patient humanness**, and a **Patient** text field through the exact Source binding. The agreement choices tell the grammar what to write around the stem. In Andrews’s **nānōz**, first-person **n** comes before **ānō**, and future **z** follows it. The **Patient** field records which participant the writer means, and its text stays outside the written form. An empty binding lists that field as required and supplies no default referent. Example Atom `ACI-P181-L013-892BAC75D4-02` gives the meaning of **nānōz**. The alternate-source Atoms ending in `-05`, `-06`, and `-07` belong to the passive promotion Owner and show that the same written passive can correspond to more than one active source. The text field is an application input for preserving the writer’s intended patient. Andrews’s formula supplies the agreement position. It issued **necōz** and retained the chosen patient on the exact finite application. The test illustrates the generated fields with a different stem from Andrews’s example. The exact public field sequence remains unverified. **Which Nonactive formation menu the writer sees.** The typed application can generate a selector with the same caption as the native **Nonactive formation** field. For Andrews’s **chīhua → lo**, either editor serves the choice of licensed formation at the right edge of the stem. The writer selects the formation where alternatives are licensed. Andrews’s following context determines whether final **o** is long. ## Composing a frequentative verbstem

| Control | Where and when | Action and inferred purpose | Sweep disposition |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Next VNC derivation layer | Verbal Grammar, when a derivation can be added | Choose **frequentative** to make a derived stem that can express repetition, intensity, or separately involved participants or occasions. | Retain in this pass |
| Grammar-supported formation | Conditional derivation control | Choose a licensed shape for the copied opening. Andrews compares **hueh-hue-tz-ca**, **huē-hue-tz-ca**, and **hue-hue-tz-ca** based on the same stem. The choice changes what the writer puts immediately before the stem. | Retain in this pass |
| Reduplications | Conditional frequentative Grammar group | Choose **one**, **two**, or **three** copying steps where offered. The count describes copies added before the base. Canvas §27.2 note 2 illustrates two added copies in **chō-chō-chōca**. A third added copy has no exact example cited here. | Retain in this pass |
| Reduplication target | Same group | Identify the material to repeat. Canvas contrasts copying the stem opening in **pah-pāqui** with special patterns that reduplicate an object pronoun (§27.3). | Retain in this pass |
| Initial i in copying | Same group | Choose **Ordinary copying** or the exceptional **Copy supportive i as real**. Andrews §27.2, note 1 contrasts ordinary **tla-(cui-hcuil-o-ā)** with exceptional **tla-(ih-ihcuil-o-ā)**. The choice changes both the copied prefix and the stem opening. | Retain in this pass |
| Meaning focus | Frequentative Grammar for the short-vowel-plus-h formation. The patient option is hidden and disabled for an intransitive Source. | With **pāqui** and short-vowel-plus-h copying prepared, choose occasions for Andrews’s **pah-pāqui**, ‘be very glad on various occasions’. The copied **pah** is written before **pāqui**. The scope choice describes the interpretation of that sequence. [Canvas §27.1](../../ANDREWS_TRANSCRIPTION_CANVAS.md#L9026) · [Example Atom `ACI-P243-L022-8073555D61`](../ANDREWS_ATOM_LEDGER.json) · [Scope rendering](../../src/ui/rendering/surface_authority.mjs#L2977) · [Patient visibility](../../src/ui/rendering/surface_authority.mjs#L3029) | Retain in this pass |

**When the next layer is required.** If an exact verbal continuation requires a `lateOperation` choice, the renderer shows **Choose the next VNC derivation layer** as the prompt, requires a selection, and hides **No added layer** in that state. The writer has already prepared the base and is choosing what change to make to it. In Andrews's **pāqui → pah-pāqui**, the new layer adds **pah-** to the left of the retained stem even though the decision comes after preparing **pāqui**. The available formations depend on that captured base. The renderer establishes these prompt conditions. The exact prompt and selection sequence for this example remain unverified in the public browser. [Canvas frequentative example](../../ANDREWS_TRANSCRIPTION_CANVAS.md#L9026) · [Continuation prompt and availability](../../src/ui/rendering/owner_journey_presentation.mjs#L4058)

**What the frequentative choice adds.** Atom `ACI-P243-L022-8073555D61` records the change from **pāqui** ‘be glad’ to **pah-pāqui** ‘be very glad on various occasions’. The frequentative Owner's prefix rule is indexed by `ACI-P243-L003-BFF719FF1B-09`. The same Owner records intensity and multiple occasions in `ACI-P243-L003-BFF719FF1B-04` and `-07`. These explain why **Meaning focus** can ask what changes in meaning while the formation rule places the copy at the left edge. The **pāqui** example illustrates both meanings. The exact options offered to the writer remain an implementation question for this Source. [Canonical Atom ledger](../ANDREWS_ATOM_LEDGER.json) · [Frequentative Owner](../../src/core/classical/nuclear-owner-specs/classical-frequentative-verbstem-domain.mjs)

**Written order.** In **pah-pāqui**, the writer starts from **pāqui**, and the result places the copied **pah-** immediately before it. In **tla-(teh-tequi)** the original object precedes the copied stem opening. The Grammar controls gather choices about the copy and reading after a Source is identified. The exact current click order and eligible values still need browser verification. The retained frequentative suite supplies a runtime reconstruction check for an ordinary frequentative and exercises target-dependent requests.

[Canvas frequentative meanings and stem examples](../../ANDREWS_TRANSCRIPTION_CANVAS.md#L9007) · [Canvas object-pronoun reduplication](../../ANDREWS_TRANSCRIPTION_CANVAS.md#L9102) · [Control definitions](../../src/ui/shell/classical_shell.mjs#L4067) · [Runtime fixture](../../src/tests/reader_frequentative_reload.test.mjs#L6)

**Copying boundary.** Andrews explains that ordinary copying drops supportive **i** before two consonants. Exceptionally, the writer can have it treated as real. The evaluator requires a supportive Source for that exception and checks the two-consonant environment. Note 2 also explains recursive copying for emphasis, illustrated by **neh-neh-nemi** and **chō-chō-chōca**. That supports a repetition choice in principle. The public availability of each count and treatment for each Source still requires a browser check. [Canvas §27.2 notes 1–2](../../ANDREWS_TRANSCRIPTION_CANVAS.md#L9087) · [Control options](../../src/core/classical/vnc_late_operation_ui_contract.mjs#L520) · [Evaluator checks](../../src/core/classical/vnc_lessons27_29_33_closure.mjs#L2634)

**Where the copying choice takes effect.** With **tla-(ihcuil-o-ā)** already prepared as a supportive-i Source, **Ordinary copying** gives **tla → cui → hcuil-o-ā**. **Copy supportive i as real** gives **tla → ih → ihcuil-o-ā**. The **Source initial i** decision still describes the base. The copying choice controls what the writer puts inside the derived stem after **tla**. The renderer offers it for ordinary frequentative variants with a supportive-i Source and excludes the fused-**tla** and mainline-reflexive targets. Atom `ACI-P245-L009-06579CE5B8` gives the ordinary rule and `ACI-P245-L017-41EC51211E` gives the exception. Separately, Atom `ACI-P245-L022-10D44EC6B3` records **chō → chō → chōca** as emphatic recursion. It supports a count choice where licensed. Public option availability for these examples remains unverified. **Counting added copies.** With **chōca** prepared, Andrews's emphatic **chō → chō → chōca** gives the writer two added openings before the base. The **Reduplications** selector has **one** as its default and offers **two** and **three** in the UI contract. The renderer shows it for ordinary short-glottal, long, and short variants and for the two root-stock variants. The contract cites the same recursion passage for all three values. Atom `ACI-P245-L019-9EDDCEF008` records recursion, and `ACI-P245-L022-10D44EC6B3` records the two added copies in the crying example. The control counts copies added before the base, giving three written instances of **chō** in total when the writer chooses **two**. The **three** menu value comes from the interface contract. The Owner validates integer counts from 1 to 32 at its input boundary. That bound alone establishes neither a public option above three nor an Andrews example for every accepted count. The separate count-boundary suite passed, including preservation of the requested count through the finite Result. The public count selection for **chōca** remains unverified. **Choosing the part to copy.** **Reduplication target** offers **lexical stem**, **fused tla**, **fused tla and lexical stem**, or **mainline reflexive**, subject to the Source. With **tla-(cōhua)** prepared, copying the lexical stem places **coh** after **tla**. In the related fused shopping stem, Andrews gives **tlah → tla → coh → cōhua**. The **fused tla and lexical stem** target names the two copied locations. For **molpia**, partial reflexive copying writes **m → oh → o → lpia**, and the plural example ends in **h**. The initial **m** occurs once. Atom `ACI-P245-L040-2E226BDA67-07` records the further copying in the shopping stem, and `ACI-P246-L002-FBADB0781E` records the supportive-i restriction for the reflexive case. **Leaving the frequentative reading open.** In Andrews’s **tē → tla → mah → maca**, the copied **mah** can accompany giving to several people or giving a variety of things. Both readings have the same written sequence. Atoms `ACI-P243-L025-2EBFB1A503-05` and `ACI-P243-L025-2EBFB1A503-07` record the two readings. **Meaning focus** is shown for the ordinary short-glottal variant. Its contract offers **leave the reading open**, **repeated action**, **separate agents**, **separate patients**, **separate occasions**, and **separate places**. The evaluator requires a typed object for **separate patients**. The focused Lesson 27 fixture passed with a typed object on **maca**, and it rejected **separate patients** on intransitive **chōca** and a focused occasion reading on the long-vowel copying route. This corroborates where the writer has a meaningful option. The open reading preserves the written copy and lets later context resolve its meaning. [Focused scope fixture](../../src/tests/classical_lesson27_groups_1_3_jobs.test.js#L77) The two **maca** readings illustrate why context can matter after the writer has settled the spelling. They do not establish that the menu identifies recipient and thing given separately. The exact public options and resulting interpretation for this two-object Source remain unverified. **Changing both edges of a root-stock stem.** In **Grammar-supported formation**, the option **destockal intransitive** represents the special derivation in Andrews’s **patl-ā-ni → pa-patl-a-ca**. The writer chooses the formation after identifying the base. On paper, **pa** goes to the left, the stock vowel is written without its macron, and **ca** takes the place of **ni** on the right. For **destockal causative**, Andrews gives **tla-(chay-ā-hu-a) → tla-(cha-chay-a-tz-a)**. The written **tla** remains first, **cha** precedes the stock, and **tz-a** goes at its right edge. Atoms `ACI-P246-L018-D3CFC041A8` and `ACI-P247-L012-1203D4C6AB` assign these changes to the respective Owners. The formation option requests the whole pattern. The grammar supplies the stem changes together. Exact public selection of these two variants remains unverified. [Canvas §27.4.1](../../ANDREWS_TRANSCRIPTION_CANVAS.md#L9139) · [Canvas §27.4.2](../../ANDREWS_TRANSCRIPTION_CANVAS.md#L9179) · [Atom ledger](../ANDREWS_ATOM_LEDGER.json) · [Formation option contract](../../src/core/classical/vnc_late_operation_ui_contract.mjs#L198)

**Reading a completed tz-a stem in context.** **Grammar-supported formation** includes **tz-a: applicative interpretation** and **tz-a: causative interpretation**. Andrews gives **tē → po → pol → o → tz → a** for speaking to someone in a barbarous tongue. The ending stays **tz-a** as context resolves its force. Atom `ACI-P248-L008-9A048EB133` assigns the contextual choice to the ambiguity Owner, and `ACI-P248-L009-6775680259` records the example. The evaluator retains the stem when it recognizes a completed **tz-a** Source and records the selected force. The applicative branch also specifies a target valence, so the same stem can enter different participant structures. The code establishes those distinctions. Public availability of either option on this exact Source remains unverified. **Selecting a formation with an uncertain or unattested base.** **Extinct or fused destockal** works from a recognized completed **ca** or **tz-a** stem. Andrews gives **po → pō → ca** ‘emit smoke’ with a reconstructed historical base. The writer can start with the surviving stem, including its long **ō**. Atom `ACI-P247-L027-850EE9B04A` records that some members survive only as frequentatives. **Uncertain ca type** is another option in the same formation menu. Andrews gives **cha → chal → ca** for speaking loudly in anger or gaggle calls. The opening copy and the suffix are visible even though the full history is unclear. Atom `ACI-P248-L032-BDAF6A2854` records the formation with **ca**. The evaluator distinguishes an eligible completed destockal shape from an eligible uncertain-ca root shape. These entries explain the intended choice. The public path for the two examples remains unverified. **Other formation choices with uncertain ancestry.** With **pa-pach-ca** as the curdling example, **uncertain ca: causative tz-a** identifies the counterpart analyzed as **tla-(pa-pach-tz-a)**. Andrews gives the traditional written realization **tla-papatza**. For the growling example, **uncertain ca: applicative tz-a** treats **tē-** or **tla-** as an object marker before **hua-hua-l-tz-a**. **Uncertain ca: fused tla** puts **tla** inside the stem for ‘bark’. This can preserve the written letters while changing the boundary the writer intends. Atoms `ACI-P249-L010-2E9F293B46-06` and `ACI-P249-L002-CFC1B3542A-02` and `-03` record the spelling and fusion facts. **Uncertain tz-ca type** represents a different pattern. With **cui-ca** as the base, Andrews writes **cui → cui → tz-ca** for a bird twittering. Atom `ACI-P249-L017-1E45355D51` records the final-syllable replacement and copying rule. **Continuing from a completed frequentative stem.** **Destockal applicative** asks to turn a prepared **tz-a** stem into the **ch-i-liā** form. In Andrews’s cutting example, **tē** goes before the retained **tla**, followed by **co-cot-o**, then **ch-i-liā** at the right. The added participant is the person for whom the cutting happens. Atom `ACI-P248-L010-87F2AADF80` assigns the suffix change to the applicative formation Owner. **Destockal type-two causative** asks for the less common pattern illustrated by **chi-chin-a-ca → tē-(chī-chin-a-qui-l-tiā)**. The replacement ending is **qui-l-tiā**, and the person affected is represented before the stem. Atoms `ACI-P248-L025-226E6B2A58` and `ACI-P248-L027-848EC806A3` record the pattern and attested example. The evaluator checks the appropriate base for each operation. **Formation contrast.** For the stem **hue-tz-ca** ‘laugh’, Canvas glosses the short-vowel-plus-**h** form as ‘smile’, the long-vowel form as ‘laugh heartily’, and the short-vowel form as ‘laugh a lot’. ## Adding a verbal matrix

| Control | Where and when | Action and inferred purpose | Sweep disposition |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Matrix stem | Verbal compound Grammar | Supply the second stem in the written compound. In Andrews's connective-t example, **yā** is the movement matrix following the eating embed. | Retain in this pass |
| Captured compound’s next role | Verbal compound continuation from a captured Result | Use the saved compound as the first or second piece of a new compound. Andrews's example adds wanting to the already compounded act of going along eating upon arrival. The existing compound goes before **nequi** in the new stem. | Retain in this pass |
| Matrix class | Verbal compound Grammar for the second stem | Identify the matrix's verbstem class. Andrews's Class A-2 **temō** example illustrates why the class matters for the form of a governing stem. The class itself occupies no written position. | Retain in this pass |
| Subject animacy | Main verbal Subject controls. The separate compound field is hidden and disabled by the current compound renderer. | Identify the referent's animacy. In **Cactoc in calli.**, the house is nonanimate. The compound request reads the main Subject frame. | Retain in this pass |
| Possessed predicate | Accompanying-possession field defined by the shell and hidden in the current compound renderer | Supply the nounstem for the thing carried or worn. In **Nochīmal yetinemi.**, the possessed shield expression is written before the verbal compound. | Retain in this pass |
| Possessor (accompanying possession) | Same hidden field group for accompanying possession | Identify whose thing accompanies them. In **Nochīmal**, **no-** is written immediately before **chīmal**. | Retain in this pass |
| Compound meaning | Captured connective-t compound continued into honorific or pejorative Grammar | Specify separate events or one idiomatic meaning. In Andrews's idiomatic **Ōquincuitihuetz.** ‘He attacked them’, the honorific formation changes **huetz** on the right and adds reflexive material before the compound. | Retain in this pass |
| itz embed meaning | Conditional verbal compound Grammar | Identify whether the written **itz** means **look or observe** or **come or go**. Andrews explicitly distinguishes the homophonous stems. The choice supplies the identity of the first piece before a compound is built. | Retain in this pass |
| Use syncopated t-ā | Verbal compound Grammar with a **yā** matrix | With **cuah** prepared before **yā**, request the shorter join **t-ā** in **Nitlacuahtāz.** The choice acts between the eating and movement stems. [Canvas connective-t example](../../ANDREWS_TRANSCRIPTION_CANVAS.md#L9505) | Retain in this pass |
| Event order | Verbal compound Grammar with **huetzi**, **ahci**, or **ē-hua** with motion **itz** | With the breaking embed and falling matrix prepared, **matrix event first** gives ‘it fell and broke’ in **Ōtlapāntihuetz.** On paper, the breaking stem is still written before the falling matrix.
