## Revising a constituent of an accepted Result

| Action in the renderer | Availability and inferred purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Part | Under **Work with Result**. Select the exact whole or a recognized constituent as the piece to revise. |
| Change | When the selected part has a supported replacement workflow, capture it and open the choices for revising it. The revision is staged against the accepted whole. |
| Add | When the selected part can accept an attachment, start an edit that keeps the exact selected part as input. In the §17.4 route, start with **Ōquittac.** and supply the already prepared **Petoloh**. The name is written to the right of the verb. |
| Use as adjunct | On a **Prepared material** card during **Add**, **Ask about this**, or **Address someone**, when the other exact Result has the required adjunct binding. Stage the prepared piece in the open adjunct role and move focus to the relation choices. In a direct address such as **Tlā xihuāllauh, Tlālīxcapān!**, the prepared name can occupy the position after the command. |
| Remove | For eligible attachments, stage a revision to the retained expression. The code requires an exact remaining Result, such as the principal of a supported adjunct construction. |
| Reorder | In **Work with Result** after selecting a part. The renderer requires both an Owner offer and a compatible edit path with multiple order values. Current ordinary supplementation fails the edit-path check for this action. The intended use is to move a prepared clause before or after its partner, as in the two **Petoloh** orders below. |
| Order | Appears after a supported reorder is staged. Choose **Principal first** or **Supplement first** from the available Owner values. |
| Unavailable actions | Disclosure shown when one or more actions cannot be offered. Open it to read the reasons for the disabled **Change**, **Add**, **Reorder**, or **Remove** actions on the selected part. |
| Ask about this | Under **Continue composing** in Result when the exact Result has a supplementation-principal binding. Open the path for supplying an interrogative clause as adjunct. Andrews’s **Ahmō tiquitta in ca nehhuātl nicmati in quēn ōmochīuh?** illustrates a written interrogative clause within a larger sentence. Exact use of this shortcut for that sentence remains unverified. |
| Address someone | Under **Continue composing** in Result when a direct-address principal binding is available. Begin with the accepted directive and supply the person addressed. In the §56.5 runtime example, the page reads **Tlā xihuāllauh → comma → Tlālīxcapān → !**. |
| Leave clause implicit | Under **Continue composing** in Result when the selected Result has a deleted-principal dependent binding. Begin from the clause of saying that the writer intends to leave understood. In §19.6, supply the surviving reply and quotation, which appear consecutively on the page. |
| Undo | Invoke the available history Undo action. |
| Clear | Under **Workspace actions** when an accepted workspace Result is available. Clear the whole active build so the writer can start a new typed Source. |

**Changing the selected part during a revision.** The public control here is **Part**. When the writer selects a different target, the Result pane sends an internal cancel action that clears its pending Result edit and refreshes the choices for the new target. This lets the writer redirect an edit to the intended piece of the accepted line. The pane's button list has no separate **Cancel** entry. This behavior is verified in the selection and edit handlers. Its browser transition during an active edit remains unverified. [Part handler](../../src/ui/composition/result_actions.mjs#L112) · [Selection callback](../../src/ui/composition/sentence_composition.mjs#L94) · [Pending-edit handler](../../src/ui/rendering/owner_journey_presentation.mjs#L2941)

**Choosing an occurrence by its role.** **Part** labels each eligible item with its grammatical role, any enclosing roles, and the written form when available. The option stores the path to that occurrence in the accepted whole. A focused renderer test reused one exact Result in two roles and confirmed that the menu kept the occurrences independently selectable. Andrews's **in cocoxqui → ōhuetz → in itozqui** illustrates the writing need from another angle. The two outer pieces jointly supply the subject of the middle verb, and the adjoining decisions can reuse the middle clause once. This motivates showing the role and page position when the writer chooses what to revise. The renderer test uses a constructed two-role fixture, and the eligible **Part** entries for Andrews's exact discontinuous example remain unverified. [Canvas and Owner evidence for discontinuous supplementation](#choosing-what-a-supplement-refers-to) · [Part label and path](../../src/ui/composition/result_actions.mjs#L118) · [Occurrence test](../../src/tests/result_actions.test.mjs#L214)

**Starting a fresh line or stepping back a build.** **Undo** and **Clear** sit under **Workspace actions**. They remain available according to whole-workspace state even when a continued Source has no selected **Part**. **Undo** delegates to History’s available undo action. **Clear** drops the active Source, prepared material, and pending edit, opening a blank writing space. By comparison, **Remove** in the selected-part group is a proposed deletion that needs Make. For **Calaquih in tēmictizqueh.**, removing the eligible attachment would leave **Calaquih** as the intended line. Clearing would start a new line. The accepted Purpose replay did not offer the adjunct as a selectable Part. This contrast describes the intent of the controls and the current handler, with the exact removal limitation recorded below. [Canvas and Purpose example](#marking-a-purpose-clause) · [Workspace action fallback](../../src/ui/composition/result_actions.mjs#L78) · [Clear and Undo handlers](../../src/ui/rendering/owner_journey_presentation.mjs#L2907)

**Backing up at three points in the writing process.** With **Calaquih** prepared and **in tēmictizqueh** staged, **Reset choices** restores eligible field values in the current draft. **Undo** invokes the same action as **Undo last build** in History and recovers the actual parent of the accepted build when available. **Clear** opens an empty workspace and returns Source derivation to its direct starting mode. These controls serve reviewing a choice, returning to an earlier accepted line, and starting a fresh line, respectively. The current handlers establish the distinction. The Purpose example locates the pieces in the written line. ### Result edit test boundary

**Current Result action test boundary.** Changing **Part** selects the role path. The organizer’s selection callback then cancels the previous pending edit and clears its requested action. A subsequent edit click separately checks what the Owner offers for the selected piece. For the repeated-clause example below, this means choosing which occurrence to work on before requesting a revision. The latest Result action suite ran 18 tests. Ten passed, including separate occurrence selection, action grouping, and staging optional outer-attachment removal. Eight failed, including the combined selection-and-edit-callback check, the pending Reorder menu, and several Change and Undo action checks. The fixture replaces the interface projection with a mock that supplies `viewExact` and omits `inspect`. Rebuild checks use `inspect` to verify exact captures. In a temporary copy that forwarded `inspect` to the real runtime, 13 of 18 tests passed. The native Undo availability, stale-action recheck, and current Change projection tests recovered. The other five failures remained. This isolates a fixture issue for the three recovered tests. Public behavior remains evidenced by the separate browser receipts. [Temporary harness probe](/tmp/ui-intent-result-actions-inspect.test.mjs) · [Capture verification](../../src/ui/composition/result_edit_rebuild.mjs#L13) [Selection and action handlers](../../src/ui/composition/result_actions.mjs#L85) · [Selection cancellation](../../src/ui/composition/sentence_composition.mjs#L94) · [Result action tests](../../src/tests/result_actions.test.mjs)

| Remaining simulation gap | What supports the inventory entry |
| --- | --- |
| Part selection followed by Change | The occurrence-selection check passes separately. The combined callback check fails, so exact Change execution after selecting an occurrence remains unverified by that fixture. |
| Accepted native Change feedback | The current-projection and click-recheck test passes. The separate simulated confirmation message check still fails. |
| Pending Reorder Order menu | The menu stays hidden in the simulation. The fresh rebuild check and retained public replays establish unavailable states for the documented constructions. The enabled menu is described from code. |
| Combined Change, Reorder, and mirrored Undo action emission | The combined test emits Undo without the expected Change. The separate native Undo availability case passes with the actual inspect projection. |
| Ready Add alongside Reorder and Remove | The fixture still does not enable the expected action. The retained naming replay independently verifies Add availability and disabled Reorder for its accepted line. |

These findings close the evidence classification for the inventory. The failing simulations remain open as test evidence. This report makes no availability claim about an enabled positive state based on a failed simulation.

**Selecting an occurrence and revising it are separate steps.** **Part** can list two occurrences that share one exact Result, using their different paths. The current rebuild helper searches by that Result identity and requires one matching path. If it finds both, actions that depend on rebuilding the surrounding whole can be unavailable even after the writer selects a specific occurrence. Andrews’s repeated-clause example **Zan īc in → auh → zan cān in itto** illustrates why occurrence matters. The reduction leaves the first repeated clause silent and keeps the second written. The conjunction’s dedicated **Repeated clause** choice handles this construction. The repeated-identity Result test is a separate fixture and verifies only selection. It and the named action-group test both passed. The exact Result edit path for Andrews’s example remains unverified. **Canvas and writing order.** Andrews §18.1 describes an integrated supplement placed before the supplemented clause. This motivates recording supplement position as a grammatical decision, separate from the action of selecting a target on the Result card. In a supported reorder, the writing decision is which constituent goes first. The implementation obtains available orders from the captured supplementation contract and only stages the requested revision. The exact public labels and a representative before-and-after Result are pending browser verification. Canvas §18.1 establishes the meaning of preposition here. It does not establish that every supplement can switch order.

**Moving a clause and moving its prefix.** In Andrews's §18.1 pair, the supplement comes first in both forms. The first form puts antecessive **ō#** before the verb. **Ōnihiyo nicān.** puts the same prefix before the supplement. Atom `ACI-P158-L003-00987D4FE7` assigns the placement rule to the integrated antecessive supplementation Owner. The **Order** selector applies to the relative position of the clauses. The separate **Antecessive placement** selector applies when the captured clauses license moving the prefix to another carrier. [Owner decision](../../src/owner/classical/clause_relation_organ.mjs#L3949) A writer revising this example needs to see which unit carries **ō#** before accepting the change. **Reading the Order options.** After **Reorder** is staged for an eligible part, **Order** starts with **Choose order** unless the staged choice matches an authorized option. The pane labels the two supported values **Principal first** and **Supplement first** and filters out other order values. In the shield example **Nochīmal yetinemi.**, **Supplement first** puts **nochīmal** before **yetinemi**. That is the order verified by the shield runtime probe. The example explains the label, and the probe used staged Grammar instead of the Result edit selector. The latter’s exact browser activation remains open. A written-form cue beside **Order** could show which piece each role name refers to. **What moves in the two Petoloh examples.** In §17.3.1 Andrews writes **Nicuīca → niPetoloh**. In §17.5 he writes **NiPetoloh → nicuīca**, with the first piece now serving as the topic. The first-person subject of the singing clause still refers to Peter in either order. Atoms `ACI-P153-L002-C48230781E` and `ACI-P156-L004-C79FB73939` support the clause and reference analyses. This is the writer’s reason to choose a placement. The position of the prepared naming clause changes while the shared subject stays the same. **When a staged revision is ready.** **Reorder** initially records the accepted order. Choosing that same value leaves the revision unready and gives the Make button the caption **Choose a different placement**. The **Order** field itself requires both a pending reorder and a currently available reorder capability. If the capability is absent, a pending action alone cannot expose the options. A blank **Choose order** appears only when the field is offered and no staged value matches its options. The proposal becomes executable only with a different supported order and the same exact selected occurrence in the still-accepted whole. **Remove** instead requires that the live target still points to the same retained Result, such as the principal that would remain after detaching a purpose clause. For the writer, these are two different points of commitment. Choose a new order for a move, or identify the part to delete, then use **Make Result** for the proposed revision. The readiness rules come from code. The exact public Reorder sequence and the Purpose removal remain unverified. **Reorder availability and focused check.** To offer **Reorder** for a selected constituent, the presenter requires an exact Owner action, a supported unique path in the accepted whole, and multiple supplementation orders from a controller rebuilt from the captured parts. The order values must also be allowed by the accepted-action projection. In §18.1 this identifies the whole-constituent move separately from changing the carrier of **ō#**. Five focused Result action cases ran in the current worktree. Two passed, covering omission of unsupported actions and optional outer-adjunct removal with stale-root rejection. Three failed. **Order** stayed hidden in the pending-Reorder case, the action-emission case emitted **Undo** without the expected **Change**, and a ready-Add case did not enable the expected action. A fresh run of the full Result-actions file passed 10 of 18 cases. The focused rerun of the pending-Reorder case again stopped at the hidden Order field, before asserting its option captions or change event. Those fixture results leave the activation sequence open. **Removing an adjunct versus leaving out its introducer.** Andrews gives **Calaquih in tēmictizqueh.** and explains that **in** may be absent in this purpose pattern. The edit-target check gives an eligible outer adjunct a removal destination at the exact principal and gives the separately displayed marker no generic removal destination. The Purpose draft already has **Clear marker** before Make. It clears the captured marker from the draft. The confirmed composition still has to pass through Make. **Remove** on an eligible accepted part instead stages an edit against that exact accepted root and child, with the retained principal as the proposed replacement. On paper these actions correspond to crossing out one word or crossing out the entire following clause. The browser coverage for those actions differs as described below. On the accepted browser Result for this example, **Part** offered only the whole. ## Looking up the grammar while writing

| Control | Where and when | Action and inferred purpose | Sweep disposition |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Find a fact | Grammar fact inspector, where exposed | Search by Atom, lesson, or wording. For example, the ordering rule for **ah# → ō#** gives a writer a reason the two chosen prefixes appear in that order. | Retain in this pass |
| Matches | Same inspector, after a query returns results | Select the relevant fact. | Retain in this pass |
| Show fact | Same inspector, after choosing a match | Reveal the statement and its source for consultation. This is a reading action with no position in the written expression. | Retain in this pass |

The shell marks the inspector as explanatory. The Owner still authorizes the expression produced through Make. The **ah# → ō#** rule above is a relevant example of the evidence a writer may want to consult. In a separate isolated **Analysis → Grammar** run, entering the exact prefix-order Atom ID `ACI-P090-L015-70557C348A` returned zero matches and disabled **Show fact**. This establishes a lookup gap for that exact query. The Canvas and the canonical ledger still document the ordering rule, and the accepted **Ahōmicqueh.** run verifies its written realization. [Grammar fact controls](../../src/ui/shell/classical_shell.mjs#L4590) · [Inspector handling](../../src/ui/rendering/result_persistence_presentation.mjs#L3556)

**Isolated browser observation.** From an empty workspace, I opened **Analysis → Grammar**, entered `ACI-P069-L035-91475DC064-02` in **Find a fact**, and clicked **Show fact**. The article displayed **§5.5.2**, the fact that tense has a present feature, and Canvas lines **2637–2639**. The query supplied the matching entry without a separate selection in this run. This verifies a public reference lookup, before choosing or making any expression. [Canvas tense categories](../../ANDREWS_TRANSCRIPTION_CANVAS.md#L2637)

**How a search becomes a reference reading.** **Find a fact** searches for one substring across the prepared Atom ID, Canvas section and line span, statement, and Owner identifier. It ignores case and normalizes equivalent Unicode spellings while preserving vowel-length marks. **Matches** shows at most 100 entries labeled by Atom ID and section. The picker keeps the current match if it survives the search and selects the first match otherwise. **Show fact** opens the validated projection of that match. This explains why the successful tense lookup above needed no separate picker action and why a zero-match query disables **Show fact**. The search and selection rules come from the renderer. The positive and negative browser lookups above establish those two public outcomes. [Fact search and selection](../../src/ui/rendering/result_persistence_presentation.mjs#L3563)

**Possible improvement to Find a fact.** When the writer is reviewing **Negative** and **Antecessive**, Andrews’s ordering rule answers which goes first. The current inspector searches a prepared set of presentation routes, and the exact ledger ID returned no match. Exposing the existing prefix-order Atom through **Find a fact** would give that lookup an answer. A link from any staged prefix readout could open the same fact if the presentation route is available. Both are design inferences. The writer still chooses which prefixes to request, and Andrews fixes their sequence. ## Reading the accepted analysis

| Control | Where and when | Action and inferred purpose | Sweep disposition |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Analysis (Result disclosure) | Result information menu, when analysis content exists | Open the grammatical explanation attached to the accepted Result. The separate top-level Analysis mode changes the workbench detail. | Retain in this pass |
| Derivation, composition, and evidence | Result in the rule-logic renderer when an authorized derivation explanation can be projected | Open the supporting details for the derived verb. The renderer places **How this result was built** inside it. | Retain in this pass |
| How this result was built | Result for a verbal derivation with an authorized derivation projection | Open the explanation of the formation. In **temō-huiā**, the first piece is **temō** and the formative follows it. | Retain in this pass |
| Formation | Inside the derivation explanation | Inspect the authorized formation steps and their effect on the written stem. | Retain in this pass |
| Participants, scope, and later voice | Same explanation | Inspect how the derived construction relates participants to the written form. Andrews’s applicative **temō-huiā** can introduce the thing descended, such as stairs. | Retain in this pass |
| Possible typed Sources / Object roles | Same explanation, when the renderer receives alternative analyses or a contextual role reading | Inspect the available analyses of the accepted expression. This disclosure presents explanations for reading. | Retain in this pass |
| [Participant] referent in this context | Result under **Possible meanings** when an Owner reading needs a contextual referent | Say what the participant refers to. The selector offers **Not specified**, applicable referent kinds, and **A different referent**. Andrews's **xīni** can describe a wall collapsing or a mountainside sliding or collapsing. The contextual setting changes which explanation the Result can show. The written stem stays **xī → ni**. | Retain in this pass |
| Reading to show | Same Result section when the exact form has multiple possible readings | Choose a supported explanation or **Leave the reading open**. An option needing another context is disabled and says **add matching context**. The controls update the interpretation view for the accepted form. **Reading the derivation across the whole clause.** In the accepted verbal derivation explanation, **Whole-VNC transformation** compares the source formula with the derived active formula. Matched colors in **Participant history** trace the same participant across both formulas. **Rule scope** explains the dependency, and **Higher layers** displays the derivation before later voice. **Returning to a required field.** The rule-logic Result shows **Go to [field]** only when the current block reason maps to an available control. For an applicative-object diagnostic the caption is **Go to Applicative object (added)**. In the **Nitlehco** continuation, that field represents the participant added by the applicative. Its object marking belongs before the stem in the written verb, so returning to the field revisits an earlier part of the expression. The recovery action opens Source or Grammar and any enclosing disclosures, then attempts to focus the field. The button resolves the target again when clicked. If no target can be focused, it reports **The required control is not available for this Source.** When focus succeeds, it asks the writer to select the highlighted field. Other mapped captions include **Source stem**, **Initial i**, and **Grammar-supported formation**. The writer still makes the choice and applies it. The retained applicative snapshot shows the object field, while the recovery button and its focus behavior come from code. Each shows the button only when the diagnostic resolves to a usable control. This makes the shortcut a way back to the missing draft choice. **What a recovery button actually confirms.** When building a **Go to [field]** button, the renderer checks that the destination is usable within its own stage, even if the writer is currently looking at another stage. For **Go to Initial i**, this returns the writer to the analysis of the vowel at the start of the stem. If focus fails, the status says **The required control is not available for this Source.** The action supplies navigation. The writer still has to make the choice. **Generated recovery captions.** The renderer prefixes **Go to** to the first available field’s listed name. The 30 explicit names are **Source stem**, **Initial i**, **Meaning focus**, **Reduplication target**, **Subject**, **Mood**, **Tense**, **Class**, **Grammar-supported formation**, **Source voice**, **Source nonactive formation**, **Imported subject (causer)**, **Causee Valence**, **Specific shuntline object**, **Applicative object (added)**, **Construction**, **Reading**, **Voice**, **Next voice layer**, **Following voice layer**, **Nonactive formation**, **Source VNC Valence**, **Object**, **Antecessive ō#**, **Honorific particle**, **Adverbial modifier**, **Introductory particle**, **Before introductory**, **After introductory**, and **Plural ending**. These names describe the caption map. A particular diagnostic and draft determine which field is available. If that field has no mapped caption, the button reads **Go to required information**. For example, the lexical noun class diagnostic points to the noun class field, which has no explicit name in this recovery map. In the writing flow, the helper can return the writer to the beginning of a stem (**Initial i**) or to a choice at the end (**Plural ending**). The target field supplies the grammatical decision. **Reading Stem relation in the table versus choosing it in Grammar.** In the **Calli.** paradigm, **Stem relation** is a column. Andrews describes the affinity copy **cā-** for houses of one village and the distributive copy **cah-** for separately located houses or different kinds of houses. The paradigm lists those spellings for inspection. To choose which meaning the line should express, the nominal Grammar has a separate editable stem-relation field whose alternatives come from the nominal option contract. The native **Stem relation** field was hidden in the public ordinary-noun draft, which instead showed the exact-binding selector **Stem Formation**. In two fresh Chrome sessions, apply **cal**, choose **Make a noun clause → Animacy → nonanimate**, then select **Stem Formation → affinity** or **distributive-varietal**. Explicit Make produced **Cācalli.** and **Cahcalli.**, with Linear showing **cā-cal** and **cah-cal**. Thus the editable selector makes a new line, while **Output scope** displays related forms alongside the already accepted line. **Where to look for the control and the table.** The shell places the native **Output scope** selectors in **Result view** and gives the paradigm output a separate section. The nominal renderer can move the scope wrapper back to Result while it groups other fields under Grammar. The surface renderer exposes **Full NNC paradigm** only when the surface is nominal, its scope is full paradigm, and both the paradigm and its visual model are authorized. The ordinary accepted-application renderer instead asks for the exact Result’s **accepted-paradigm** projection. These are separate presentation paths in code. An authorized table in a fixture establishes the projection it exercised. The replay observation above establishes whether the writer had a selector to open it. **Where the scope should follow the saved line.** The accepted-Result renderer reads the scope field for the family of the accepted application. The verbal surface renderer also has its own visibility rule tied to the basal Source unit. Those paths establish separate inputs for rendering a paradigm and showing a selector. The **Calli.** replay above establishes the visible mismatch. It leaves open which update last set the selectors after hydration. A design inference is to make the existing **Output scope** control follow the accepted Result when the writer is inspecting a saved line. For **Calli.**, that would put the noun’s available related forms within reach without asking the writer to re-enter **cal**. **Returning from a paradigm to the line.** **Output scope** asks for the paradigm of the exact accepted application. On an authorized projection the renderer hides the primary single-form display and inserts the paradigm, while keeping the Result body and actions. On an unavailable projection it leaves the primary display visible and shows the availability guidance. This accounts for the browser still showing **Nihcac** after the full-paradigm request failed. Returning to **single form** selects the view of that one expression. The code establishes the rendering rule. The cited browser run exercised the unavailable branch. **What the paradigm groups let the writer inspect.** The accepted-Result renderer requests the Owner's paradigm for the current application. Where it receives one, the first group opens initially. The writer can open another group for nouns by state and, where applicable, possessor. Verbal groups are organized by mood and tense. The captions come from the row values, so the first nominal group can simply read **Absolutive**. The renderer opens the first group on initial display. Opening a later group reveals its rows for reference. The verbal per-cell disclosures described below come from a separate renderer. Nominal rows show subject, stem relation, plural ending, and written form. Verbal rows show subject and form. This lets the writer consult related forms without changing the subject or ending of the accepted line. Where the Owner supplies no paradigm, the accepted-Result renderer says **A paradigm view is unavailable for this Result. Its single form is shown.** This is guidance to continue from the accepted line or use **single form** to return to that display. The note itself has no action. The saved **Nihcac** browser receipt documented a different unavailable message, and it did not exercise switching back to **single form**. Both the fallback and the grouping rules here come from code. **Looking up a form and returning to the draft.** In the accepted-Result paradigm, each written form is a text cell. For Andrews’s **ticihuātl** and **nocihuāuh**, the lookup helps locate **ti** or **no** before **cihuā** and the ending after it. A row click would be a different action from inspection and would need a separate design decision. The read-only rows and scope behavior are verified in the renderer. Returning to **single form** displayed **Calli.** again. This confirms that the writer can open a possessor reference group alongside the original state and then return to the accepted line. **Which paradigm renderer owns the view.** The accepted-Result **Output scope** handler requests the exact Result’s `accepted-paradigm` projection. **Reading a revision inside a word.** With **quēzqui** prepared, the writer chooses the distributive/varietal formation. The reviewed word begins **quē → c → iz → qui**. The copy goes inside the existing word, and the spelling of the preceding **z** changes to **c** before the copied **i**. That spelling follows from the formation. The **Grammar analysis** disclosure has a concrete purpose here: it can show why the writer has to revise the inside of the word before writing the next piece. ### Analysis formats

| Control | Where and when | Action and inferred purpose | Sweep disposition |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Analysis / Structure and analysis | Accepted Result when at least one analysis child is visible. The disclosure renderer uses **Structure and analysis**, and the organized browser view shows **Analysis**. | Open or collapse the grammatical explanation for the current line. | Retain in this pass |
| Linear | Result, when the Linear format is available | Inspect an analysis in sequence. In the ordinary **Iz tihuītz.** receipt, the two constituent formulas appear in written order. | Keep the accepted-form view |
| Diagram | Result, when the Diagrammatic format is available | Inspect the grammatical structure. The §52.7.1 drum analysis is an example of separating the clauses and showing their grammatical contact. | Keep the relationship view |
| Sentence | Result, when the Sentence formula is available | Inspect the sentence-level formula, including material outside the clause such as **ah#** and **ō#** in the §8.1 example above. | Keep the sentence view |
| Specific | Structure and analysis, when a specificity switch is rendered | Inspect the actual morphs and stem of the accepted form. This is the default. | Retain in this pass |
| General | Same switch, enabled for the cited projection when a general formula and diagram rows exist | Inspect the grammar pattern with slots in place of particular morphs. This helps a writer see where comparable material would go in another expression. | Retain in this pass |
| Formula annotation buttons | Linear, Diagram, and the rule-surface Sentence formula where the presenter supplies annotations. In General for **Micqueh**, the browser showed **subject person**, **nominative**, **predicate stem**, **mood and tense**, **number connector**, **subject number**, and the clause, position, subposition, and stem boundaries. Diagram also showed **nonsubject constituents**. | Open the explanation for the selected slot or mark. Click it again or press Escape to close the explanation. For the written **Micqueh**, the stem is **mic**, followed by the ending **queh**. Andrews's general formula shows where the number connector and subject number fall after the stem. The earlier slots describe grammatical structure even when they contribute no written letters. | Retain in this pass |

**Reading a compound join after Make.** On an authorized nominal compound, the formula renderer can offer explanations for the first stem’s realized shape and boundary. In Andrews’s **malacatl**, the compound-only explanations describe **ma** and **il-aca**, and the supportive-vowel explanation identifies why the written sequence is **ma → l → aca → tl**. The specific supportive-vowel cue requires the omission frame. The Owner fixture’s retained-vowel comparison **mailacatl** has no such frame, so this cue is unavailable there. The first-stem shape explanation can also show a stem’s source class and resulting letters. [Omission and retention assertions](../../src/tests/reader_compound_matrix_supportive_i.test.mjs#L7) These annotations read the accepted operation. The writer edits the underlying choices through the compound fields in Grammar. The annotation builder places each cue on an available formula character, so the explanation can describe a different position from the character that opens it. The exact spindle annotation clicks remain unverified. [Canvas §31.6 and spindle Owner evidence](#choosing-the-relation-within-a-nominal-compound) · [Compound annotations](../../src/ui/rendering/formula_presentation.mjs#L1902) · [Cue placement](../../src/ui/rendering/formula_presentation.mjs#L1874)

**Opening formats together.** **Linear**, **Diagram**, and **Sentence** are individual disclosures for available projections. The renderer wraps each visible format section using its title, **Linear format**, **Diagrammatic format**, or **Sentence formula**, as the match. It opens the first matching visible section in the supplied order. Hidden sections do not get a format toggle, and the whole **Structure and analysis** disclosure is hidden when all its children are hidden. Other visible children can keep that outer disclosure available even when there is no Linear or Diagram toggle. This explains why the outer **Analysis** label alone does not establish which views are available for the exact line. The writer can open another format to trace the same piece in more than one display. For **Ahōmicqueh.**, Linear places **ah#** and **ō#** before the verb formula, and Diagram labels their separate functions. Both explain the same accepted line. Opening a disclosure changes what the writer can inspect. The browser receipt confirms both formats for that Result, and the disclosure structure and initial opening rule come from the renderer. [Analysis disclosure and format construction](../../src/ui/rendering/result_presentation.mjs#L219) · [Accepted browser formats](#negative-and-antecessive-browser-record)

**When Analysis mode keeps formats open.** The public organizer holds the outer **Analysis** disclosure and its available **Linear** and **Diagram** disclosures open in Analysis mode. It saves the open state of each disclosure node the first time that node is forced open, marks the summary unavailable for toggling, and cancels clicks on that summary. Returning to Simple restores the saved state of each surviving node. If a Result redraw replaces a disclosure, the replacement starts with its own rendered state. **Sentence** is outside this automatic-open selector and follows its own disclosure behavior when offered. For **Ahōmicqueh.**, the two available views let the writer read **ah → ō → micqueh** and inspect the layered structure without switching formats. These mode-specific toggle conditions are from the organizer. The retained receipt confirms both available views for the accepted line. [Analysis mode disclosure behavior](../../src/ui/composition/composition_presentation.mjs#L54) · [Disclosures included in the mode](../../src/ui/composition/composition_presentation.mjs#L279) · [Browser evidence](#negative-and-antecessive-browser-record)

**Boundary buttons in the accepted sentence.** The Linear snapshot for **Ahōmicqueh.** shows **negative assertion** on **ah**, **nuclear clause boundary; attaches right** on the first **#**, and **nuclear clause boundary** on the next **#**. It also shows **subposition boundary** on **-**, **position boundary** on **+**, and **statement** on the period. Andrews writes the analytical sequence **ah#ō#Ø-Ø(mic)Ø+qu-eh#**. In ordinary writing the prefix letters and verb form appear together and the period closes the sentence. The boundary buttons help the writer inspect the joins and internal divisions without adding punctuation to the written word. The browser recorded the labels and their positions. The explanation action is supported by the annotation renderer. Clicking **negative assertion** on **ah** displayed the explanation “negative assertion” and set the button’s expanded state. **Escape** removed the explanation and collapsed the button. **Enter** reopened it. The writer can thus check what the initial **ah** does while reading the written sequence **ah → ō → micqueh → period**. This interaction verifies the prefix annotation on the replayed build. The Sentence formula is produced separately. The clause-relation **Canonical composition** panel uses annotated formula glyphs for a supplementation frame and plain formula text for its other relation results. This is specific to that panel. **Moving between formula explanations.** Each annotated glyph acts as a button. The renderer allows one explanation at a time. Activating the same glyph again closes its explanation. Activating the next glyph closes the earlier explanation and opens the new one. **Enter** or **Space** activates the focused glyph, and **Escape** closes its explanation. In **Ahōmicqueh.** the writer can check the explanation for **ah** and then inspect the adjoining boundary before reading on to **ō** and **micqueh**. The browser verified click, Escape, and Enter on **ah**. The toggle and switch behavior come from the renderer. **Specific annotations for Micqueh.** The isolated browser snapshot before making the negative sentence showed two controls around **mic** in Linear. The opening parenthesis was named **miqui** and the closing parenthesis **miqui keeps this stem shape**. The source code uses the closing annotation to describe the chosen Source valence and retained stem shape. On the page, **mic** precedes **queh**. The clickable parentheses belong to the analysis of that stem, and the annotation action opens its explanation. The snapshot confirms the labels and positions of the buttons. The explanation behavior comes from the renderer. **Written order and available views.** For **Ahōmicqueh.**, the retained browser receipt records **ah# → ō# → (mic)** in Linear. Diagram names the negative and antecessive prefixes separately before the verbal nuclear clause. Both views also appeared after address replay. The current specificity switch redraws Linear and Diagram while using the same accepted Result. The projection fixture expects the abstract nuclear formula **#pers¹-pers²(STEM)num¹-num²#** separately from the sentence-level prefix stack. Its current run stopped before these assertions because the test context could not call the projection helper. The receipt establishes the displayed sequence. In a fresh local browser session, I opened the saved **Ahōmicqueh.** and selected **Analysis**. **Specific** was pressed and **General** was disabled. I then opened the saved plain **Micqueh** and clicked **General → Specific**. In General, both Linear and Diagram exposed slots including **pers¹** and **STEM**. Returning to Specific restored the specific view. The accepted **Micqueh** remained displayed throughout. [Retained browser receipt](#negative-and-antecessive-browser-record) · [Specificity controls](../../src/ui/rendering/result_presentation.mjs#L232) · [Accepted projection](../../src/ui/rendering/owner_journey_presentation.mjs#L10227) · [Sentence-layer fixture](../../src/tests/panel_sentence_layer_analysis.test.mjs#L19)


**Why General can be disabled.** The accepted-Result renderer enables **General** when the projection supplies both an abstract Linear formula and general Diagram rows. It redraws those two views on a switch. The separate **Sentence** formula is outside that update. In the retained contrast, **Micqueh** showed the abstract stem and ending positions, while **Ahōmicqueh.** kept **Specific** as the available view. For a writer comparing the left-edge prefixes, this means continuing to read the exact **ah → ō → micqueh** sequence in the available analysis. The browser establishes the enabled and disabled states for those two Results. The current renderer establishes the general availability rule and which views the switch redraws. The separate verbal, nominal-construction, and relational-noun renderers also require both components before enabling the same **General** button. The switch begins with **Specific** pressed and updates the pressed state only for enabled choices. Which components are supplied depends on the exact projection in each view. **Which view a fresh switch starts in.** Selecting **General** changes the currently mounted switch and its formula and diagram. The constructor initializes each fresh switch to **Specific**. A direct event probe on the shared constructor verified that **General** becomes pressed when enabled, a new instance starts with **Specific** pressed, and a disabled **General** does not call the selection handler. The probe used simulated elements. A writer returning to the abstract **Micqueh** layout may need **General** again if reopening the Result rebuilds the switch. The probe establishes the new-instance default. Retention across ordinary panel navigation remains unverified. ## Standalone design previews

The repository contains two directly addressable design previews. Their controls illustrate how a writer could inspect or stage retained examples. The behavior below comes from their markup and scripts.

| Preview and controls | Placement, availability, and purpose |
| --- | --- |
| **Classical Nahuatl**, **Your path**, **See saved builds** | On the guided preview, the brand links to the current page fragment. The two path buttons open the same session drawer. |
| **Retained example**, **Use this source** | The Source selector offers the whole quotation, principal, and adjunct. Changing it reveals the apply button and disables **Make sentence** until the selected example is applied. |
| **Composition**, **Compose options**, **Make sentence** | Grammar lets the writer stage the quotation or either constituent. The disclosure opens the preview’s notes about the particle and draft. Make displays the selected prepared line. With the quotation selected, the written principal comes before the quoted adjunct. |
| **Copy**, **Whole sentence**, **Principal**, **Adjunct** | The Result tools copy the displayed line or select which part the continuation menu refers to. After making a single constituent, only **Whole sentence** is enabled. |
| **Continue composing**, **Use as source**, **Add an adjunct**, **Ask a question** | The disclosure opens the three actions. Each changes the operation heading and status, then focuses **Composition**. The writer can inspect the proposed next move in the preview. |
| **Analysis**, **Linear**, **Diagram**, **Sentence**, **Show labels**, and formula or written-part buttons | The Result disclosure offers the three views. The checkbox adds labels to the formula buttons. Those buttons explain individual marks, and **Sentence** adds clickable written parts that identify the principal and the quotation. |
| **More actions**, **Reset this preview** | The Result disclosure includes **See saved builds** and the reset button. Reset reloads the preview. |
| **Close Your path**, **Saved build**, **Whole sentence**, **Principal**, **Adjunct**, **Use as source** | In the drawer, choose a retained build and a part. Selecting a standalone build disables its constituent buttons. **Use as source** stages the chosen preview text and closes the drawer. |
| **More**, **Branch from this**, **Compare builds**, **Undo last build** | In the drawer, the branch button updates the preview’s status. Compare reveals or hides the prepared comparison. Undo restores a prior preview acceptance when the session has one. |
| **Andrews’ formula and structure**, **Linear**, **Diagram**, **Sentence**, **Grammatical details** | The separate Sentence Analysis preview uses disclosures to display retained specific and general analysis for its sample. These let the reader inspect the written form and the roles in its formula. The captured formula markup includes 61 focusable cues marked as buttons, with tooltips describing their positions. The standalone HTML loads no script to activate those cues. Its seven native disclosure summaries are the working controls supplied by the markup. |

**Static-page coverage check.** The tracked page entry points are the workbench, Privacy, the missing-page fallback, the two design previews, and the search verification file. The verification file and plain-text Security destination have no page controls. The Sentence Analysis preview has seven disclosures. **Andrews’ formula and structure** contains specific **Linear**, **Diagram**, and **Sentence** views plus general **Linear** and **Diagram** views. **Grammatical details** is a separate disclosure. The guided preview’s native buttons, selects, checkbox, and disclosures are accounted for in the table. Its formula and written-part buttons are added by script. Captions and conditional availability in the table come from the markup and handlers. The retained runs below establish selected drawer behavior. **Quotation in the guided preview.** Its prepared **Ca quihtoa, “Ca nichōca.”** illustrates the visible order **reporting clause → comma → quoted clause**. The preview’s **Composition** menu chooses among three existing strings. Andrews’s §19.6 reply example instead gives the live **Speech relationship** choice its purpose: the writer decides between direct and indirect presentation while keeping the captured material in its grammatical roles. In the direct fixture the writer reads **Niquinnānquilia → comma → quoted Ca nehhuātl niyez.** The preview helps illustrate that layout. The Canvas passage and live Owner fixture supply the authority for the reply construction. [Canvas §19.6](../../ANDREWS_TRANSCRIPTION_CANVAS.md#L6699) · [Direct and indirect quotation fixture](../../src/tests/reader_deleted_saying_quotation.test.mjs#L14) · [Guided preview choices](../../prototypes/apple-guided-design/index.html#L5)

**What Undo restores in the guided preview.** In isolated Chrome, choose the reporting clause in **Composition** and press **Make sentence**. The preview displayed **Ca quihtoa.** and disabled the two constituent buttons. Open **Your path → More → Undo last build**. The quotation **Ca quihtoa, “Ca nichōca.”** returned, with the reporting clause still before the quotation, but **Principal** and **Adjunct** remained disabled in Result after the drawer closed. The script restores the earlier accepted string and redraws its formula. The scope enablement update is in the Make handler. **Compare builds** likewise toggles a prepared comparison, and **Branch from this** changes the status text. These describe the preview’s controls and state. [Preview Undo receipt](/tmp/ui-intent-preview-undo.json) · [Preview handlers](../../prototypes/apple-guided-design/design.js#L5)

**Keyboard route in the guided preview.** In isolated Chrome, clicking **Your path** opened the dialog with focus on **Close Your path**. **Escape** closed it and returned focus to **Your path**. Reopening the drawer and selecting **Use as source** closed it and moved focus to **Composition**. The last transition puts the writer at the next choice after retrieving an already prepared line. This observation applies to the standalone preview. [Browser focus receipt](/tmp/ui-intent-preview-dialog.json) · [Dialog markup](../../prototypes/apple-guided-design/index.html#L9)
